data.text: With the anti-gun-rights crowd and their political axis in Congress cashing in on "terrorism" as their new watchword for gun control, our liberties are at stake as never before, They are using "terrorism" as an excuse to enact universal gun owner registration and for laws that criminalize all now-legal, private intrastate firearms transactions - meaning all sales, trades, gifts - between peaceable persons. If you own a gun, they want your name in a computerized Federal database-profiling you on the basis of mere ownership of a firearm. Prior to the September 11 World Trade Center and Pentagon attacks, the likes of Senators Charles Schumer, Ted Kennedy Dianne Feinstein, Hillary Clinton and Joseph Leiberman were all too willing to let Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain take the lead - thus keeping the ire of gun owners focused away from their party until after the next election cycle. But with every anti-gun-rights group now reading off the same page, and the media shrilly echoing their demand for gun registration and new firearms bans, the Schumers, Feinsteins, Kennedys and Bradys have taken the bit as never before. Terrorism has become the vehicle reviving a far-reaching agenda to destroy Second Amendment freedom. Arizona Sen. John McCain, still leading the charge on the phony issue of "the gun show loophole," has promised his media followers he will force a Senate vote on gun control soon. Count on the rest of the antigun rights crowd piling on - like Ted Kennedy demanding that National Instant Check Records on approved, cleared firearms purchasers be kept and made available to a wide range of law enforcement, The Kennedy legislation would make the lists available to cities for "civil" purposes. Read lawsuits. (See the "ILA Report" on p. 76.) McCain's absurd claims about terrorists and gun-shows are backed by a massive national propaganda campaign paid for by monster.com billionaire Andrew McKelvey through McKelvey's slick lobbying group, Americans for Gun Safety (AGS). The AGS headlined its big lie: "Terrorist Access Makes Gun Show Background Checks Important to America's Security." When you blow away the fog of disinformation and lies supporting the so-called' 'gun show loophole," you clearly see the creation of universal firearms registration - the mechanism for future selective confiscation of private arms from the American people. The leadership of Handgun Control, Inc. - hiding behind its new name, the Brady Campaign to End Gun Violence - is not even talking about "regulating" private sales at gun shows any longer. They now demand "requiring a check every time a firearm is sold." And they insist "Congress should also ensure that federal law enforcement has a record of every firearm sale ... (Emphasis added.) That leads us to the Violence Policy Center (VPC). Tie VPC's demand for strict Federal records on lawful firearm transactions to the organization's end game - criminalization of all now-lawful handgun ownership, coupled with confiscatory laws on many forms of long guns. The creation of permanent records of gun sales on a Federal database, however it might come - from Ted Kennedy or John McCain - is the big step to the final step - confiscation of your private property It has already happened here in America - in California. The Brady Campaign celebrated when they forced law-abiding gun owners - who had registered their long guns - to abide with the ultimate gun law and turn their firearms over to police to keep from being prosecuted. If private gun commerce by violent criminals or drug dealers or fugitives from justice - or ILLEGAL ALIENS - is McCain's target, keep in mind that all gun commerce by such persons - anywhere, anytime, under any circumstance - is already covered by a host of Federal criminal statutes. Simple gun possession by prohibited persons is a Federal felony - 10 years in a Federal prison. Foreign terrorists? It is a Federal felony for an illegal alien to "ship or transport in interstate or foreign commerce, or possess ... any firearm or ammunition"; or to "receive any firearm or ammunition." That covers everything everywhere. A prohibited person's mere presence at a gun show could be construed as a Federal crime. And if any person acquires a firearm with the intention of violating other laws - antiterrorism laws, for example - that act is covered by tough Federal penalties as well. McCain's so called "gun show loophole" legislation - S. 890 - does absolutely nothing to cover activities by criminals at gun shows. In fact, the words "felon," "criminal," "terrorist," or "prohibited person" don't even appear in his legislation. It won't make what criminals or terrorists might do at gun shows any more illegal. It will make what we do illegal. We are the target. We will be the victims. We will be profiled on government computers. You must act now to stop McCain's, Kennedy's and Feinstein's big-lie legislation. Write your Senators and U.S. Representative. Call their offices. E-mail them. Tell your friends and neighbors to do the same. Our Nation's 70 million firearms owners are not terrorists, and we must never pay the price for what evil people do. No new gun control. No gun show closedown. No retention of records. Period.

When the founders of the National Rifle Association of America banded together in the Fall of 1871, the first object for the Association set forth in their charter was "the improvement of its members in marksmanship." Having set the goal, they wasted no time in trying to reach it. They raised the funds, they found a site and, before the year was out, work had started on the famous Creedmoor Range of shooting history, a range that for many years was to rank as the best and most modern in this country and abroad. It was officially dedicated on June 21st, 1873, by the firing of a Regimental Team Match in which twelve teams competed. Nine of these came from New York and one from New Jersey representing National Guard units from those two states, and the other two from Regular troops in the immediate vicinity of New York City. The success of these matches attracted attention far beyond the boundaries of New York State. By 1877, the States of California, Louisiana, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York and the District of Columbia were represented with teams at Creedmoor, while the individual matches drew competitors from all parts of the Union, Canada and foreign lands. Not only was the organization carrying out its stated purpose of improving its members in marksmanship; it was already embarking upon the broader program of creating a public sentiment and an awakened interest in the matter of rifle practice throughout the United States. In the meantime, another momentous step had been taken. Within a year from the time the first shot went down the range, the National Rifle Association pioneered in the field of international sporting events by playing host at Creedmoor to a rifle team from Ireland. That was more than a decade before the first of the modern Olympic Games of 1896. From its very beginning, the National Rifle Association has promoted friendly rivalry between nations in the sport of shooting. Scarcely a year has passed, except in time of war, that we have not engaged in some sort of an international competition, either postal or shoulder to-shoulder, with high power or smallbore rifle or with pistol. As a member of the United States Olympic Association, NRA is recognized as the organization which governs the sport of rifle shooting in America. For the past many years it has represented all the shooters of this country, both rifle and pistol, before the International Shooting Union. It was solely because of our efforts that the United States was represented in the World's Rifle and Pistol Championships in Oslo, Norway, in 1952, and most of the burden of supporting our entries in the Olympic Games fell on our shoulders. This year will mark another milestone in the field of international shooting when the World Championship events will be fired in Venezuela under the auspices of the International Shooting Union. These Matches will take place in December. An NRA International Shooting Committee has been appointed and plans are already undo way for selecting and holding both rifle and pistol teams to represent this country in those events. The teams will be larger and, we anticipate, better organized, better trained and better equipped than those we sent to Norway two years ago. In giving them our support, the NRA is carrying on a tradition that is as old as the organization itself. The sport of shooting is a character builder. There must be coordination of mind and body. A good shooter is a judge of the elements and master of himself. He must determine with each shot what windage to use, if his elevation is correct, and the exact moment to give that final squeeze of the trigger which sends the shot down the range. He must be a good loser as well as a good winner if he is to remain at the top. There is a camaraderie between shooters that is found in few other sports. This is true not only between members of a single team but between teams representing different nations as well. The rifle and pistol team which represents this country in the 1954 World Championships, therefore, will be good will ambassadors to each of the fifty-one other nations which may be represented there. The competition will be a friendly one, but serious nonetheless. Each shot that is fired will be a test of the man, of his equipment and of his training. Win or lose, the net result will be that we have improved our members in marksmanship. The knowledge the team acquires will benefit us as individuals, as an Association and as a nation. Let us give them our moral and financial support.

Americans, for the most part, come from a long line of honest, hard-working ancestors who were optimistic enough to believe that they could, if given a fair chance, build a better life for themselves and their children no matter how tough the initial going. They succeeded. So Americans are born optimists. They hide it under a lot of critical, cynical, rough-and-ready talk but they really find it hard to believe that any nation or any sizable group can consistently devote itself to a policy of cynicism, double-dealing, and oppression. The American's congenital optimism, his faith in himself and in his fellow man, is his greatest strength and, unfortunately, his greatest weakness. It has made him the beacon light for the optimists of the world - but it has frequently made him a sucker for the cynics and double-dealers of the world. On June 19, 1948, the American Congress decided that appropriations to encourage civilian small-arms practice could safely be stricken from the Army Appropriation Bill. On July 31, 1948, the United Press reported that the Soviets hail disclosed plans for the establishment of a broad plan 'for the systematic semi-military education of Soviet youth' which includes the setting up of 'a network of rifle clubs and shooting ranges throughout the Soviet Union.' More than a decade ago when the likable, well-intentioned Attorney General, Homer S. Cummings, was urging Congress to pass a Federal Firearms Registration Act, we successfully opposed it. When we pointed out as one objection the fundamental danger to the democratic system which is inherent in the political control of the citizen's personal weapons of defense, we were asked if we thought that Attorney General Cummings or President Roosevelt would use such a law to disarm reputable American citizens and establish a dictatorship. We replied that we did not believe they would but we had no way of knowing what others in the government then or in the future might do. Any law which depends on the good intent of those enforcing it to insure fairness, justice, and continued democratic processes is bad law. Now we know that Communist infiltration into confidential and responsible positions in the American government were taking place at that very time, fitting perfectly into the pattern set by subsequent developments in Canada, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Austria, and Romania. Can any sane person now question the fact that the Moscow-directed Communist organization would like very much to have a carefully prepared official registration list of patriotic arms-owning Americans? Can there any longer be doubt that if such lists were established by law the subversive elements could obtain them without too much effort? Can there any longer be doubt that the possession of such arms registration lists would strengthen the courage and speed the plans of the lying, double-crossing gang who have already made suckers of so many Americans whose Pollyana optimism has blinded them to the facts of past and contemporary history? American optimism is still the great hope of the world but American law-enforcement officers and American legislators who discourage civilian small-arms practice, who seek to bring the reputable individual's personal defense arms under centralized political, police, or military control, are permitting their optimism to make them into suckers for the cynical, double-dealing crowd who will 'liquidate' them first of all if, as, and when the time seems ripe!

On Thursday, March 22, 1956, Lieutenant General Floyd L. Parks, USA (Retired), was elected to the position of Executive Director of the National Rifle Association of America. He succeeds Major General Merritt A. Edson, USMC (Retired), who died on August 14, 1955. General Parks' election to this post of leadership is the culmination of more than six months' work by two special committees successively appointed by NRA President Mumma. The first committee, appointed in August 1955 shortly after the death of General Edson, reported to the Executive Committee in December 1955. In January, another committee was named. This new seven-man committee - all non-paid NRA officials - first set down the duties and responsibilities of the Executive Director along with the qualifications they believed necessary to fulfill these duties and responsibilities. This afforded a workable basis for an evaluation sheet on which the qualifications of more than a score of individuals could be recorded in comparative form. After discussions and interviews were completed, the committee unanimously agreed to recommend General Parks as having the qualifications required. Accordingly, his name was offered in nomination on March 22 to the NRA Board of Directors, and he was elected by unanimous assent. The variety, magnitude, and importance of the tasks imposed upon the NRA Executive Director demand a man of broad qualification. The members of the committee - all long associated with NRA affairs as Directors and in other important capacities - put down requirements they knew must be met if the position were to be filled by an individual who would be both an outstanding leader and a representative of the Association. Heading the list of requirements were those of personality, character, vigor, and known executive ability. Next in importance were the requirements of a knowledge of public relations in the broad sense coupled with public speaking ability, imagination, writing ability, and a 'sales promotion sense'. Further requirements called for a knowledge of legislative operations at all levels, with contacts, experience, and background in the field, along with a knowledge of the military at all levels. A final but basic requirement was that the candidate selected have a knowledge of the NRA, including its aims and objectives, and believe in and support them. General Parks, a native of Kentucky, was born in Louisville in 1896. He was graduated from Clemson College in 1918 with a Bachelor of Science degree, and from Yale University in 1924 with a degree in mechanical engineering. His military career spans over 38 years, beginning with service as private in January 1918, and going through the ranks to February 1956 when he retired as a lieutenant general. General Parks' military assignments have been many and varied, including service with the Corps of Engineers, a tank battalion, an infantry regiment, an armored regiment, an armored division, an infantry division, and an airborne army. He is a graduate of the Infantry School, the Command and General Staff School, and the Army War College. During World War II he was Chief of Staff of the First Allied Airborne Army. When that Army was disbanded in May 1945, the U.S. element of it became the First Airborne Army under General Parks' command. In this position he led the first U.S. troops into Berlin. He was the Commanding General of the U. S. Sector in Berlin, a position he held until he was ordered to Washington to become Chief of the Army's Public Information Division from 1946 to 1948 and again from 1950 to 1953. In August 1953 General Parks was appointed Commanding General of the Second Army, and it was this command that he held until his retirement. The National Rifle Association of America was born of the belief that the principles of marksmanship and shooting inbred in our forefathers should forever be fostered and promoted in our country. In its 85-year history the NRA has never swerved from that basic tenet. Rather it has continually expanded its programs and services so as to bring more people to appreciate the enjoyment and benefits that can accrue to the person who learns to properly know and use firearms. A combination of imaginative thinking, a competent Staff, and decisive leadership has enabled an always-growing NRA to turn to its advantage challenges born of changing times. The membership, Directorate, and Staff can confidently expect General Parks to help them meet the challenge of these changing times.

I: Are We Really So Violent? In a syndicated year-end article at the happy holiday season, the leader of one of the many marches on much-marched-upon Washington blamed the "violence of the American spirit" for African slavery, Indian repression, extermination of the buffalo, gangsterism, the KKK and making "the gunman a hero." Two newspapers old and large enough to be grown up, in New York and Washington, prate editorially that we Americans are a violent people, brutishly addicted to mauling and murdering our fellow men. One quotes the New York City police commissioner as deploring our national violence. When the Mayor of Chicago recently asserted "we live in an age that spreads violence and hatred" and demanded an end to it, Chicago City Council heartily agreed. Two members had recently been attacked by robbers, one being wounded in the leg. Anyone battling through life in 6 of our largest cities, including Chicago and New York, may well be stunned by the crashing impact of crime. These 6 cities, with a tenth of the U.S. population all told, produced a fifth of all U.S. homicides and crime in 1966, according to the U.S. Uniform Crime Report of Aug. 10, 1967, whereas over a third of sizeable American cities reported no homicides at all. The same report indicates that if one of its statistical classifications is excluded, the homicide rate for most of the U.S. population decreases by about one half. Therefore we object, on behalf of nearly 200,000,000 Americans who have had no part in homefront violence, to sensational assertions that Americans on the whole are a violent people. Many of those who say so would brand the mark of Cain upon the nation's brow to further highly restrictive nationwide firearms legislation. In the cold light of fact, we question that such legislation is necessary. II: What Can Be Done? The upswing in violence in recent years coincides with 2 developments that the U.S. Government ought to be able to curb administratively, without firearms legislation by Congress or anyone else. One is: Television's growing incitement to murder and mayhem by abnormal, exaggerated emphasis on misuse of firearms and all manner of diabolical attacks. Ironically, some of the same networks that have smeared legitimate firearms ownership under guise of protecting the American public from guns have televised gunplay, gore and horror galore. This bombardment, if we may use the word, approaches a 7-day, 24-hour saturation of the American mind with the notion that gunplay is good clean fun. Does it really stir up violence? Hear this: "It has been found that normal persons who see a violent (televised) film subsequently exhibit nearly twice as much violence as persons who have not seen such a film." Ironically indeed, this statement was made by Sen. Thomas J. Dodd (Conn.), author of several firearms control bills including the pending S. 1. on July 30, 1964, after years of hearings before his Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Juvenile Delinquency. Dodd deplored the lack of "any serious effort" to calm down television - but no bill has yet been advanced to do so. Not everyone, it should be noted, agrees that Congressional action is necessary. Some feel the FCC could reduce TV violence by administrative order. III: What Else Can Be Done? A second definite factor in the crime increase, in the opinion of many police chiefs, is the cut-rate sale of cheap imported handguns. Shoddily manufactured by a few foreign makers, hundreds of thousands of these have been peddled in recent years by a handful of U.S. dealers. Prices as low as $8 or $10 have placed concealable handguns within reach of multitudes who never before could afford them. Most figure in "crimes of passion" or amateurish holdups, which form the bulk of the increase in violence. Again, administrative action appears to be all that is necessary. But a National Administration that cries out constantly for firearms controls has done nothing in this respect, although its own records disclose that 437,021 revolvers and automatics in .22 cal. rimfire - mostly, it should be added, of cheap manufacture - were imported in 1965-67 alone. The director of the State Department's Office of Munitions Control testified before Sen. Dodd's subcommittee last July 10 that his agency feels that the law regulating firearms imports applies "only to the extent of determining that the munitions are initially consigned to bona fide wholesalers or to individuals" for "lawful purposes." Inquiry by this magazine recently revealed that the Office of Munitions Control lacks technical experts to distinguish between firearms that come up to generally accepted U.S. standards and those that do not. It appears that a panel technically qualified to evaluate imports could be set up without an Act of Congress. As it is, the Office of Munitions Control has no official way of determining which are so crudely made that they ought to be excluded from the U.S. The Administration, however, possesses sufficient authority to bar by Executive direction these miserably-made, potentially defective arms that contribute so much to rising violence. If a few foreign manufacturers become offended, State Department diplomacy should be equal to that crisis. Here then, without the fireworks and forensics of a major issue in Congress, are 2 practical steps toward reducing violence. Both have been recognized, discussed, and-for some reason-quietly shelved. Will the Administration act now? It can, without waiting for Congress or transferring any burden of woes to that august body. U.S. Senate Hearings. Subcommittee to Investigate Juvenile Delinquency of the Committee on the Judiciary, pursuant to S. Res. 274. Part 16. July JO. 1964. Pages 3736-3737. Sec. 414. Mutual Security Act of 1954. as amended, under a delegation of power by the President to the State Department.

Soon the pulse of the hunter again will quicken at the first hint of sharpness in the air as another hunting season unfolds. But thousands will find last year's hunting grounds blocked by "NO HUNTING" signs put up by an ever-increasing number of landowners. America's tradition of hunting as a sport for all people is being sharply challenged by the pressures of modern society. With each sign posted, its end comes closer to reality. When our forefathers established our government, it was decreed that wild game belongs to the states in their sovereign capacity for the use and enjoyment of all the people. At the same time, it was decreed that the landowner has the right to determine who may come upon his land to hunt the game. While pressures were light, conflicts between public ownership of game and private control over its harvest were not critical. As the population increases, trespass laws become more restrictive even at a time when more and more people with more leisure time are depending on the outdoors to meet their recreation needs. Wildlife and its related recreation are essential parts of the total American way of life. Wildlife must be properly managed and harvested else it is doomed to extinction, and proper harvest itself provides recreation values of great importance. As custodian of the nation's wildlife, the landowner has an obligation to provide reasonable opportunities for hunting but he cannot be expected to give up his private rights and freedom from unauthorized trespass. Public hunting on private land is a privilege, not an inherent or vested right, and must be earned by proof of respect for the landowner's rights. Too many hunters are guilty of vandalism, trespassing, careless handling of fire and firearms, and violations of game laws. The true sportsmen of America cannot afford to permit this small minority group to destroy the outdoor recreation opportunities for all. Hunters must work together and with landowners to control the vandals; they must encourage good sportsmanship example; and they must insist on the highest standard of conduct from hunting companions in the field. In an effort to help perpetuate hunting as a public sport, the Izaak Walton League's Hunt America Time program for 1959 is designed to promote better hunter-landowner relations. Its theme is "Respect Private Property - Save Public Hunting". Individual hunters are encouraged (1) to be law-abiding, (2) to respect the rights and property of others, and (3) to be careful with fire and firearms. The NRA Hunter Safety Course, which emphasizes proper gun handling and sportsmanship afield, is scheduled as an important activity in the program. All hunters should actively support this effort to improve the standards of hunter conduct afield. In the final analysis, the mutual understanding between outdoorsmen and landowners will determine whether wildlife will persist in abundance and remain available to the public. The real test of hunter-land-owner relations comes in the field while hunting seasons are under way. That's where hunters must face their responsibilities, because only hunters can save public hunting on private property.

September 7th marked the end of the most successful National Rifle and Pistol Matches since 1940. On that day sixty-five rifle teams competed for the National Trophy which was first awarded by Congress in 1903 and which has been in constant competition since that date. Over two thousand individuals had participated in the small bore, pistol and .30 caliber events. Almost five hundred individuals received training in the Small Arms Firing School in how to teach marksmanship to others. One hundred and twenty-seven attended the evening sessions of the Range Officer and Referee School to learn the best methods of organizing, supervising and conducting our rifle and pistol tournaments. Practically every state and territory, every branch of the Regular Services and every walk of life were represented among those who participated in the program. Father and son, junior and oldster, the tyro and the old-timer, were all present to improve themselves in marksmanship and to learn how best to impart their knowledge to others. While still far short of the great spectacle of pre-war days, when the ranges now incorporated into the Erie Ordnance Depot permitted a concurrent firing of all three tournaments and Uncle Sam underwrote the program, it was a most heartening experience and gave promise for the future. Among the notables who visited the Matches and witnessed a part of the firing were The Honorable John Slezak, Assistant Secretary of the Army (Materiel), and President of the National Board for Promotion of Rifle Practice; General Lemuel C. Shepherd, Jr., Commandant of the Marine Corps; Lieutenant General John E. Dahlquist, Chief of the Army Field Forces, and some of the Adjutants General of the various States. Every one of them left Camp Perry convinced of the value of the Matches and their allied schools and the part that they play in the over all national defense structure. It is easy for the uninformed and the uninitiated to criticize and condemn. It is easy for one who has never seen the National Matches to refer to them as "competitive sporting events" and to the participants as "hobby shooters." It is regrettable, therefore, that many others who are directly concerned with our national defense could not have spent a few hours at Camp Perry also. If they had, they, too, would have been converted to the worthiness of the National Board program. They would have seen, for example, that over five hundred of the thirteen hundred odd competitors in the .30 caliber rifle and pistol events came from the Regular Services - the Army, the Navy, the Marine Corps, Coast Guard and the Air Force. These men were not there as "hobby shooters" taking part in a "sporting" event. They were there at the direction of superiors to increase their capabilities as instructors of others in the matter of how to hit a mark. They came from posts and stations, from ships and squadrons, from regiments and corps throughout the world. Already they have returned to these far-flung units to train, to instruct and to encourage others in the techniques of rifle and pistol marksmanship. These visitors would have seen, too, some thirty law-enforcement agencies from as many different communities throughout the country and the National Guard from sixteen states and the Territory of Hawaii represented on the firing line. Today these men, too, are home again, passing on to others the shooting lore which they learned at Perry. The same holds true for the civilian participants who came in greater number than did the serviceman, the policeman and the guardsman combined. They came for exactly the same reason - to improve themselves in marksmanship so that they might be better prepared to train others who may be called upon to serve. None of us believe that the National Board for Promotion of Rifle Practice should confine its efforts solely to the support of the National Matches as it was prone to do pre-war. None of us believe that the ability to hit the bullseye on a known distance range makes an individual a finished combat marksman. But all of us believe that these two things taken together provide a very essential element in our national defense. A man cannot become a good combat marksman until he has acquired confidence in the weapon he shoots and his ability to hit what he aims at. The National Matches are the testing ground of the marksman and of the weapon and the ammunition which he uses. There is no other place at which the Regular, the civilian, the National Guardsman and the Reserve can mingle freely to exchange ideas and to improve each other in the art of shooting. It is the function of the National Matches to produce instructors in marksmanship. It is the function of the National Board to make it possible for these instructors to pass on their knowledge to others. The Board is not concerned with the training of the men in service. That is the responsibility of the several Departments of the Armed Forces, each of which have the funding and the material means to discharge it. The Board is concerned, however, with the training of those citizens who are not in uniform but who may be called upon serve their country in time of war. The National Board and the Armed Forces, then, complement each other the common purpose of building our nation again into a nation of marksmen. There is, however, a material difference between the two. Those competitors who attended the National Matches from the Regular Services, law-enforcement agencies and the National Guard by and large had their transportation, their subsistence and their other expenses defrayed by the Service or the Municipality or the State they represented. The civilian shooter had to pay for these things out of his own pocket. When the first group return to their duty station or home, they are by and large paid for the time they spend as instructors, and the ammunition which they or their students use in training is furnished to them. On the other hand, when he picks up the burden of instructing the juniors in his community and his young friends of military age in marksmanship, the civilian does so on his own time, without remuneration and often on ranges which he himself has helped construct. Further than that, he will henceforth, because Congress has now so decreed it, be forced to purchase on his own funds the ammunition he needs to train them. The National Board was created to serve the country at large. Even though it is an agency within the Department of the Army, this program is of benefit to every Service and to the Nation as a whole, not just the Army alone. The appropriations which are made for it, therefore, should be considered as an overall Department of Defense Appropriation, not just an Army Appropriation. If necessary, the Secretary of Defense and the Appropriations Committees of the House and Senate should insist that the Navy, Marine Corps, the Air Force and the Army contribute proportionately to the $800,000 required by the Board for fiscal year 1955. The National Matches exemplify the unity of purpose of all segments of our people who believe that the ability to shoot straight is a part of the defense of our country. It is a job for the Armed Forces, the law-enforcement agencies, the reserve components and civilians alike. Only if Congress realizes this fact and supports the civilian agency - the National Board for Promotion of Rifle Practice - as it does the Armed Forces with funds adequate do its job, will we have a truly well-rounded marksmanship program.

1984 is upon us. It is well to examine the problems we face. Not a laundry list of New Year's resolutions nor yet a list of things to do, but instead a statement of issues and concerns and of problems for which solutions are sought - our goal being to provide a stronger and better informed membership that we may be enabled more assuredly to protect and further our right to keep and bear arms. Membership must exist before there can be protection of our rights and before there can be better programs we desire. We expect to pass three million members in the summer of 1984 - splendid evidence of NRA's credibility among the American people in this important, perhaps vital, election year. We have this evidence of faith and confidence in the NRA and we must merit and nurture that faith. 1984 offers opportunities for further protection, development, and viability of NRA's necessary political goals. It is election year. We must get out he vote of our membership. All eligible members and families should register to vote. This further implies reason and leadership in candidate selection, that we select for public office from among those good citizens who are mindful of our civil rights and who are insistent, as President Reagan once said, that the heavy hand of government shall rest upon law violators and not upon decent, tax-paying citizens with a lawful intent. In 1984 there will be the shooting events of the Olympics near Los Angeles. There will be additional strength in NRA's assistance to law enforcement. NRA schools are already scheduled for the Police Department of Chicago and for the Metropolitan Police of Washington D.C. An area of greatest growth for NRA perhaps is with hunters, with the legitimate and sporting use of firearms. Junior activities are being increased and the number of junior members is already greater than ever before. We came a long way in 1983 and this put us still further on the step for 1984. The ownership of firearms is a matter related to privacy and to decent purpose. The shooting sports are participation sports. The members of the NRA are participants, whether in their sports or in the exercise of their individual rights or in government. We are not spectators of the world about us. We face great complexities in 1984 serving a great and numerous membership, and especially we face the problems of communication and unity, all designed to achieve the goals which the members seek. With your help, and yours is the final help with meaning, we shall continue forthright, direct, and, if necessary, blunt reporting to you. We will call the shots as we see them, and I will accept full responsibility for giving you the truth as it is and not necessarily as we would wash it to be. There is no end to the problem of better communications - that you, the members of NRA, are fully informed as to events which come and go and can be predicted in the National Rifle Association. NRA has a number of publications. All the staff involved in them understand the need to be free of any restraint in communicating with you. The staff will continue in 1984 to serve according to the best available wisdom and with all efforts possible to represent and to support your desires. This is addressed to you the membership. You are the NRA, and you are the real and final authority in the NRA. You elect the Board of Directors who must represent you subject to your power to deny them election or re-election. We must be honest with you that you understand there are possibilities in the future of even worse perils than those we have surmounted. The greatest of these perils is evident in the existence and the activities of a small dissident minority who have proposed and supported bylaws fragmenting the NRA Headquarters into independent, balkanized fragments - none of them responsible to another - and this at a time when all the successes of the future are more than based upon unity and greater strength. And now there are those who would prevent me from reporting this to you. A calm and reasoned respect for the generations to come dictates that where there is a question of political differences, it will be thrashed out that this shall be done within the machinery of NRA and that NRA shall never be weakened by washing dirty linen in the public view or before the Congress. We can already see aa NRA of such size, of such financial strength and dedication to our cause and our course that few politicians will wish to tread carelessly upon our rights - protection and furtherance of our rights to keep and bear arms for the future if our children as it was for u and our fathers before us.

On October 9, 1950, the Court of the District of Columbia altered the oath of allegiance taken by foreign-born persons in the process of becoming naturalized citizens of the United States. To the oath was added, "I shall bear arms on behalf of the United States . . . when required by law." Yet during the legislative year of 1949-1950, as in every year since 1950, numerous bills designed in one way or another to restrict or control the right of citizens to own and use arms were introduced in state legislatures. The majority of these bills failed to become law because the expressions of opinions of voters were overwhelmingly against such measures. However, the introduction of the bills apparently indicates that a widespread number of lawmakers in state bodies hold the belief that individual citizens are not to be trusted with firearms - at least without the permission of certain political officials. While most of the legislators who introduce these measures are aghast that shooters see in their actions any idea of distrust of the individual citizen, the fact remains that the minor ills and aches of our American society which the measures are intended to cure are of far less importance than the healthy privilege to keep and bear arms which Americans have long held. It is not amiss to recall that in November 1637, before a nation had been founded on these shores and when a musket was a tool used to obtain food and protect the home, seventy-six persons in the Massachusetts Bay Colony were deprived by the General Court of "all such guns, pistols, swords, powder, shots and match as they shall bee owners of, or have in the custody" to censure them for differing in belief from the elected leaders of their Puritan community about the way in which one could attain everlasting salvation! Im light of the extensive activity among state legislatures to restrict the right of Americans to own and use arms, the oath required in the District of Columbia of adults becoming naturalized citizens of the United States seem slightly awry. It recalls a song popular a number of years ago. Remember? "Mother, may I go in swimming?" "Yes, my darling daughter. But hang your clothes on a hickory limb. And don't go near the water."

SINCE December, 1941, the core of all NRA activities has been the Preinduction Small Arms Training Program. That program was the natural thing for us to do. By reason of our traditions and our training, we were peculiarly fitted to carry on that work. It was a part tailor-made for us in the war effort. But it was fortunate for several million young Americans that the National Rifle Association had those traditions and that training! For, in spite of the sincere efforts of General Marshall and the High Command, instruction in small-arms marksmanship was tragically inadequate once the rapid expansion of our armed forces got under way. Neither rapidly trained officers nor quickly promoted noncoms had more than a superficial knowledge of how to shoot. They knew little about the underlying principles of marksmanship essential to the training of marksmen. That was nobody's fault. It was just America going to war. America, where "every man is a born rifleman," with a million of them ready to spring to arms overnight! America, where too many people thought that the rifle was no longer of much value in a war which they believed would be dominated by mechanical marvels! No one who saw the NRA schools in operation - no one who has read the letters which have come back from men in the armed forces - can ever doubt the value of the Preinduction Training Program. Men so trained have made use of that training themselves and have passed it along in other "classes," formal and informal, held all over the world, teaching the rudiments of gun handling to yet other men who, in many cases, had been sent to foreign fronts carrying weapons they did not even know how to load! These "classes" do not show on our NRA record of achievement. The dead Japs and dead Nazis who fell and are falling before the aimed fire of men who never fired a rifle before they entered Preinduction Training Classes-entitle us, back home, to no medals. And that is as it should be...But we can cherish the deep-down glowing satisfaction of knowing that we helped. And we can be very sure that the skills and traditions of fine marksmanship fostered and kept alive by the riflemen of America are playing their full part in the attainment of the victory of Allied arms. That phase is past now. As the old year ends, we look to the new year with high hope that it will bring an end to war. But war's end marks merely another milestone in the history of American marksmanship. War's end will mark the beginning of a vast revival of sport and competitive shooting throughout this nation and throughout the world. It is our job, as shooters, first, to guard our right (and the rights of men now-busy at another job) to shoot, and to prevent the infringement of that right by fanatic laws - and, second, to guide the development of that postwar revival of shooting interest into such channels that the traditions of American marksmanship "may not perish from the earth." Peace, when it comes, is not the end. It is only the beginning!

We're going to take all the guns!" - every firearm owned by good and honest citizens instantly became an "illegal gun." Our answer to the tyranny of New Orleans is a resounding NEVER AGAIN! In spite of the clear intent of Congress to end malicious lawsuits bankrupting the firearm industry, Bloomberg and his big-city allies are using their "illegal gun" scam to pursue a new spate of suits in Federal court. In her words, that's when government "recognized the inherent inappropriateness of these highly dangerous weapons and took away nearly 700,000 of them to be melted down into soup cans and bus-stop benches ..." That is what Peters' U.N. gun-ban treaty and what Bloomberg's campaign of big-lie publicity and big-lie lawsuits are all about. With the current pro-Second Amendment majorities in the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate, their dreams cannot become our nightmare. That's why in the coming Federal elections, we must make sure that this pro-gun majority remains in place. If you know Second Amendment voters who are not registered, get them signed up. If you can vote early, do so, and work to educate friends, family and neighbors that the threat to our Freedom from the Bloombergs and Peterses will become reality if one of their allies like Congress-woman Nancy Pelosi becomes Speaker of the House, and Senator Chuck Schumer assumes a leadership role in the Senate.

The year 1958 marks the centennial of the birth of Theodore Roosevelt. He probably was more active with the rifle than any other President of the United States, and certainly expressed himself more forcibly on the value of rifle shooting and rifle marksmanship than most men in public life. This attention to shooting undoubtedly stemmed from his purposeful efforts in early years to lead a 'strenuous life' in order to build up his frail body. Also, it reflects interests developed in his three years as a rancher in western Dakota. It was during this period that he expressed his belief that "The rifle is the free man's weapon. The man who uses it well in the chase shows that he can at need use it also in war. . . ." His experience in the Spanish-American War strengthened his belief in the value of accurate rifle shooting as a most important aspect of a soldier's training, an aspect that should be given greater emphasis. We find many references to rifle shooting and rifle training among his State papers. In his first annual message as Governor of New York in 1899, he spoke strongly in fav or of the adoption of the Krag rifle with its smokeless powder ammunition as the standard arm for the New York National Guard, stating that the National Guards of the various states ought to be armed with the same rifle and cartridge as the regular Armed Forces of the Nation. In his second annual message, he stated: ". . . It is very much to be wished that means could be taken to provide the most ample facilities for rifle practice. The United States must depend upon its citizen soldiery in the event of a great war. ... It would be a good thing if there were a rifle range in every village of this State. . . . Moreover, it should be remembered that target practice proper is the alphabet of the soldier's marksmanship. ... In a battle the only bullets that count are those that hit." In three of the annual messages to Congress delivered while President, Roosevelt spoke strongly in favor of marksmanship training. In his second annual message of 1902, he said. "The Marksmanship of the men must receive special attention." During his first term of office the National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice was created and the Congress provided funds for National Trophies to be awarded in annual competition. In his annual message to Congress of 1906 Roosevelt had this to say: "The Congress has most wisely provided for a national board for the promotion of rifle practice. Excellent results have already come from this law, but it does not go far enough. Our Regular Army is so small that in a great war we would have to trust mainly to volunteers and in such event these volunteers should already know how to shoot: for if a soldier has the fighting edge, the ability to care for himself in the open, his efficiency on the line of battle is almost directly proportionate to excellence in marksmanship. We should establish shooting galleries in all the large public and military schools, should maintain national target ranges in different parts of the country and should in every way encourage the formation of rifle clubs throughout all parts of the land." This statement was amplified and extended in length at the eighth annual message to Congress in 1908 as follows: "There should be legislation to provide a complete plan for organizing the great body of volunteers behind the Regular Army and National Guard when war has come. Congressional assistance should be given those who are endeavoring to promote rifle practice so that our men, the Services and out of them may know how to use a rifle. While teams representing the United States won Rifle and Revolver Champiomships of the World against all comers in England this year it is unfortunately true that the great body of our citizens shoot less and less as time go on. To meet this we should encourage rifle practice among schoolboys, and indeed among all classes, as well as in the military services, by every means in our power. Thus, and not otherwise, may we be able assist in preserving the peace of the world. Fit to hold our own against the strong nations of the earth, our voice for peace will carry to the ends of to earth. Unprepared, and therefore unfit, we must sit dumb and helpless to defend ourselves, protect others, or preserve peace. The first step - in the direction of preparation to avert war if possible, and to be fit for war if should come - is to teach our men to shoot." In 1904, President Roosevelt instituted the practice which extends to this day, of writing a letter of congratulation to the winner of the President's Match at the National Matches. In each of the letters he continuously stressed the point that "A soldier who cannot shoot is a soldier who counts for very little in battle." In 1907 he became a Life Member of the Nation Rifle Association of America. Great trends are established by men with the courage and strength to make decisions, the will to implement them, and the wisdom to select leadership to direct them. Theodore Roosevelt was such a man and can be thankful for his dynamic leadership in the movement for civilian marksmanship training.

Never before in the history of America has there been such widespread discussion of public issues as there is today. This is extremely important because our form of government depends upon enlightened and responsible citizens. Public opinion is a powerful influence and, when based on true facts and sound reason, is a source of strength for our nation. Democracy is founded upon a balance of the power of different groups rather than upon the power held by any one or by few groups. The Constitution of the United States provides for a careful system of checks and balances between various branches of government. In addition, the first ten amendments, or Bill of Rights, were added to the Constitution as a further protection of the opinions, privileges, and opportunities of individual citizens. The second of these amendments assures the right of the American people to keep and bear arms within the framework of the Constitution, and this right has been jealously guarded throughout the years. Unfortunately. there is developing in America today a public opinion which is unfavorable to this right to own firearms and use them for lawful purposes. Many factors affect the position a person will take on any public issue. Some people are well informed or make an effort to become so; others make snap judgments on the basis of casual impressions. The surest, safest, and most constructive guide for public opinion is education. The freedoms and liberties that our society provides also impose a number of responsibilities upon its citizens. If they are to discharge their responsibilities capably and in their own interests it is obvious that they must be sufficiently informed to know where their interests lie. They must be able to understand the relationships between their own individual welfare, the proposals of government at all levels, and the interests of various special groups. Then they will see through the aims and devices of those who are attempting to manipulate public opinion for selfish interests or through lack of understanding, rather than for the public good. Individuals and groups who take part in the process of public decision to see that their legitimate rights and interests are protected are good for the people as a whole. They are an essential part of the democratic process in modern society. The National Rifle Association of America, consisting of loyal Americans with diverse interests in firearms and shooting, stands as a bastion against countless attempts to disarm the citizens of this country. The strength of its members is in NRA and the strength of NRA is in its membership. Its greatest influence is due to the unselfish efforts of its members in the field of firearms legislation and it is here that the millions of gun owners have a responsibility to take an active part in the protection of their own interests. The important thing is that we bring into play the full potential of all those who have a vital interest in the right to keep and bear arms. Because union gives strength, this can best be done by enrolling them in the National Rifle Association of America. The right to keep and bear arms is a priceless heritage which must be protected from those who would impair it. Those who cherish this right should join today and build NRA. Working together, we can make known the true facts and create public opinion which is favorable to firearms and shooting.

In a film tribute at the NRA Annual Meetings in Orlando, Tom Selleck, a Hollywood star and staunch supporter of the Second Amendment in his own right, called Charlton Heston: "A man whose patriotism is a state of being. Not a brief burst of sentiment reserved for the Fourth of July, but the steady allegiance of a lifetime. A man whose devotion to principle is a primer for how to be an American patriot. "It's a lot easier to play a leading man than it is to be a leading advocate like Charlton Heston," Selleck said. "While history will judge his place in theater, we can already judge his place in the constellation of American patriots. Charlton Heston is ... Freedom's leading man." Amen to that. In the 132-year history of NRA, Chuck Heston has stood among the best ever to lead our Association - the oldest civil rights institution in America. His deeds have had a profound effect on the solidarity of our membership and on the American public's perception of the NRA. When Charlton Heston was elected to the presidency of the National Rifle Association at the NRA's 1998 Annual Meetings in Philadelphia, NRA members put their faith in not just a man, but in the spirit of freedom and liberty he exudes and to which he has devoted his life to protect. In his unprecedented five-year tenure, Chuck Heston has been effective, not just because of his status as an American icon and a Hollywood legend, but because - much like Ronald Reagan - there is an openness about him that exposes a decency and honesty that always shines through. When ordinary Americans hear him speak eloquently on his beliefs in America, they cannot help but walk away understanding and sharing his fundamental knowledge that ours is a good nation of good people, whose power stems from liberty and freedoms we are blessed to share. Tirelessly representing NRA, his plain-speaking defense of American liberty has been heard across the nation, energizing firearm owners, persuading those who first disagree with our beliefs and, ultimately, changing the course of history. In a 1997 speech before the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., he unabashedly told the standing room-only audience of reporters and editors: "I believe every good journalist needs to know why the Second Amendment must be considered more essential than the First Amendment. This may be a bitter pill to swallow, but the right to keep and bear arms is not archaic, it is as essential to liberty today as it was in 1776. "And your efforts to undermine the Second Amendment, to deride it and degrade it, to readily accept diluting it and eagerly promote redefining it, threaten not only the physical well-being of millions of Americans, but also the core concept of individual liberty our founding fathers struggled to perfect and protect. "I simply cannot stand by and watch a right guaranteed by the Constitution of the United States come under attack from those who either can't understand it, don't like the sound of it, or find themselves too philosophically squeamish to see why it remains the first among equals: because it is the right we turn to when all else fails. "Please go forth and tell the truth. There can be no free speech, no freedom of the press ... for anybody anywhere, without the Second Amendment freedom to fight for it." That was Heston at his best, unafraid to voice the views of the millions of individual Americans he represented. And he did it proudly, anywhere he could. I am grateful that we can count on him to continue as long as he is willing. Being with Heston, watching him touch the hearts of thousands of families - especially on the grueling political trail of the 2000 elections when activist supporters of the Second Amendment delivered key states to George W. Bush - was an incredible honor. He moved people by reminding them of their proud heritage in American freedom. Our freedom. Last year, even though it was an especially draining schedule, Charlton Heston was on the campaign trail again. This time he was instrumental in inspiring pro-gun-rights voters with a can-do spirit. His appearances at rally after rally in key states electrified our voters in what the media wanted people to believe was a ho-hum off-year election. Chuck Heston on the campaign trail is remarkable, yet always, in a word, humble. With NRA members, with voters, with families, he always listens, always connects. Given all he has accomplished in his life - international stardom and acclaim - he has never lost touch with his mid-American roots. Nor has he ever lost sight of what is important in life: faith, family and freedom. He is one of us - one among us. And what he is - what we are together - has never been said so well as in his words expressed in his farewell as President: "We're an amazing bunch when you think about it. Nowhere else in the world, or in the history of the world, is there a fellowship of millions devoted to the singular mission of preserving freedom from its adversaries." Along with our thanks to him, we owe a debt to his wife, Lydia, and others close to him who have made enormous sacrifices so that he could serve the NRA and the cause of freedom.

Another new season has arrived during which multitudes of hunters will be treading the countryside enjoying the thrills of stalking and bagging varmints or the small game that may be in season in their respective localities. This phase of the shooting game requires real skill; a skill, incidentally, which when achieved is transferable to the hunting of bigger game, competitive shooting, and, if necessary, military combat. Varmints and small game are quick and elusive. Living often in proximity to man, they are among the wariest of creatures. They have to be, because man is the natural enemy of them all. For the hunter, scoring a hit is highly satisfying. And, in the case of varmints, there is the additional satisfaction of knowing that animals destructive to man's property have been destroyed. Yes, varmint and small game hunting is fine sport. But in every human activity there are rules to be followed for the mutual benefit of all, and this is true of varmint and small game hunting as well as other forms of shooting. While there are likely more hunters of larger game, a great many more rounds are fired at the smaller live targets, if for no other reasons than that varmints and small game are more numerous and more accessible. They abound in cultivated, more densely populated areas - on farms and on the unused land that so often borders cities. The possibility of accidents and damage is obviously inherent in these circumstances, and accidents and damage do occur. Each year there are instances of gun accidents involving hunters and innocent bystanders. There are cases of damage to houses, barns, farm machinery, fences, and other property. Livestock is sometimes shot accidentally. There are altogether too many cases of hunting game out of season, which is not only contrary to sound conservation principles but also dangerous. There are occasions on which hunters have committed the sin of hunting on a farmer's property without first obtaining his permission - a discourteous and perilous practice - have been sufficiently numerous that today great numbers of acres of good hunting land are posted. Few of these incidents need have happened. Nearly every one of them has been the result of negligence born of a lack of knowledge. It is doubtful that many members of the NRA have been guilty of breaking the rules. We know and appreciate their value too well. We are bonded together to uphold the highest standards of gun safety and sportsmanship. But are we doing all we can to influence others outside our fold toward proper behavior as hunters? As the leaders in the shooting field it is our duty to do so; and when one considers that the number of members in the NRA is less than one-fiftieth the number of persons who hold hunting licenses in the United States (14,000,000), the magnitude of our responsibility becomes most apparent. Since its inception in 1871, the NRA has been vitally interested in the field of firearms safety education, and throughout the eighty years of its existence the Association has given constantly increasing attention to the development of this facet of its work. Time and time again it has demonstrated that education, not more restrictive firearms legislation, is the solution to any gun problems which now exist. The specific application of gun safety instruction to hunters had its beginning in New York State in 1949 with legislation was passed requiring that young hunters receive instruction in the use of firearms before being issued the first hunting licenses. Shortly thereafter, because this educational work was overburdening the State Game Protector, the NRA was designated to give instruction and issue the certificates required by New York State law. A course of instruction and other necessary materials were prepared by the NRA, and the work of instructing was taken over by qualified NRA members. Since this program was instituted comparatively few hunting accidents have occurred and the nearly 900,000 New York State citizens who annually hold hunting licenses. Now, as the result of the great success of the New York State program, several states are interested in initiating similar programs. The NRA has attempted to provide groups and individuals in other parts of the United States with some guidance in hunter safety procedures. So favorable has been the reaction that the NRA has prepared for acceptance on a nationwide basis a revised and more elaborate version of its original NRA New York Hunter Safety Course which will be ready for distribution in the near future. All evidence points to a steadily widening interest in the idea of hunter safety education on a state-wide, legislative basis. But component organizations and individual members of the NRA also have at all times a clear responsibility to educate those non-members about them who participate in hunting, to advise them and encourage them to follow sound hunting practices and to develop their sometimes later instincts of sportsmanship. Bear in mind that for you as one NRA member there are fifty non-member hunters, many of whom do not have the knowledge one should have if he is legitimately too call himself a hunter and a sportsman. In the period ahead, some of the latter will be in the woods and in the fields in your area, hunting varmints and small game while at the same time thoughtlessly endangering themselves and others and doing needless damage. It therefore will be an extremely worthwhile contribution if you individually, or in cooperation with other members in your organization, see to it that as many as possible of these hunters - especially the younger ones - are given an opportunity for hunting instruction before they go afield. If hunting is to become a completely safe sport, and we are to prevent the enactment of more restrictive measures against guns, remember: hunter safety education is never out of season.

INTO the office comes a small slip of paper, a much smaller slip of paper than is required for the writing of an ordinary letter, but it sets in motion a large train of events. Out of the office go telegrams - one, two, a half-dozen, perhaps. In a distant state capitol telegrams are received and read. A telephone call or two, a few conferences, and another antifirearms bill is dead - buried in one of those committee files which form the mausoleum of so much legislation that began life in high hope and with much fanfare of publicity. And back at the Headquarters of the N.R.A., in Washington, where the little slip of paper was first received, business continues on the even tenor of its way - teaching Young America how to shoot safely; organizing civilian rifle clubs; encouraging the police to shoot criminals instead of innocent bystanders. And all the while, out in the state in which an antifirearms bill has just died, the individual members, and even the club secretaries probably, do not realize that such a bill has been introduced at their state capitol. This is no dream of a shooters' Utopia. It is a concise picture of what has been going on day after day in this country since January. It is a picture of actual conditions, and accomplishments made possible not by any black magic or nocturnal "lobbying" on the part of the officers of the N.R.A., but by careful building, conscientious cooperation, wide-flung organization, and a frequently-exhibited willingness and ability to bring down upon the head of the short-sighted antigun legislator the concentrated wrath of a considerable portion of the folks "back home" upon whom he is dependent for reelection. There has never been a year in which the National Rifle Association has been more successful in taking care of the legislative interests of its members. There has never been a year when the work has been accomplished so quietly. There has never been a year when the members have stood in greater need of the guardianship of the Association in legislative fields. The continued cooperation of the rifle and pistol shooters of America in the functioning of their national body during the past two years has made the N.R.A. one of the outstanding organizations of the depression period. Today, with some forty state legislatures in session, the shooters are reaping the harvest of their continued support of America's oldest national sportsman's organization.

In November, 1952, General John R. Hodge, then Chief of Army Field Forces, said this: "In the early days of the Korean fighting, one outstanding lesson was learned - every man must be trained to fight as an infantryman first, then to perform as a specialist in his respective branch. There were, and are today, in Korea daily instances where men in all units the of the combat zone have been called upon to defend their positions against infiltration and guerrilla attacks. . . . "Repeated incidents in World War II also pointed out the value of infantry training for all soldiers. On many occasions, men other than infantrymen were called upon to fight on the front lines when infantrymen were not available. Today, one of the first things the new soldier learns is that he must be primarily a fighting man, ready at any time to enter combat. His later training, even at advanced levels, will be based on that fundamental principle." The fundamental principle enunciated by General Hodge has been the basic tenet of the National Rifle Association since its origin. When General Hodge speaks of an infantryman he is referring specifically to a rifleman. The rifle is the fundamental arm of our fighting forces. In the final analysis the rifle is the intimate companion of the one whose life must depend upon it and his ability to use it. Like General Hodge, I have stoutly maintained that the need for training every individual how to shoot straight is greater today than at any other time in our history. The task of seeing that our youth are taught how to shoot before they are inducted into the Armed Services and that they maintain their proficiency with their individual weapons after they have served their stint belongs to the National Board for Promotion of Rifle Practice and to the NRA. It is the task which Congress spelled out for the National Board when it was formed in 1903. It is the task which Congress delegated in part to the NRA in the cognate acts of 1924 and 1927 relating to the National Defense Act of 1916. It is the task which the Armed Services, in spite of the billions of dollars appropriated to them, have never yet proven themselves capable of carrying out. It has been reported that 10,000 rounds of small arms ammunition had to be expended to wound one of the enemy in the Korean conflict. It took five times that amount to kill a Communist soldier. And only one in five soldiers or so ever bothered to fire their rifles at all. This is a far cry from the days of the Minute Men at Lexington and Jackson's backwoodsmen at New Orleans. This is a sad commentary on the infantry training program. It is a glaring example of the wastefulness that results from the misguided theory that volume of fire is an effective substitute for accuracy of fire. It is an indictment of those who send our youth into battle without adequate preparation There is evidence aplenty that, given adequate encouragement and financial support by Congress, the National Board for Promotion of Rifle Practice, through its civilian agent, the NRA, can teach our youth how to handle their individual weapons properly and can maintain that ability throughout the span of years they are eligible to serve in the defense of the nation. While the miserly amount of $100,000 which Congress appropriated last July will keep the National Board alive throughout the fiscal year 1954, it will not begin to permit it to perform the task for which it was created by Congress. The faulty thinking regarding the functions and the inherent capabilities of the National Board is evident in the remarks contained in the Report submitted on June 27, 1953, by the Committee on Appropriations of the House of Representatives in connection with the Department of Defense Appropriation Bill for fiscal year 1954: "It is the sense of the Committee that the National Board should spare no effort in attempting to make available .22 caliber ammunition to the junior rifle clubs, and should, in fact, do its utmost to encourage the junior clubs." We have no quarrel with the Committee's concern relative to the junior rifle clubs and the training of our youth of preinduction age. We of the National Rifle Association arc primarily responsible for the success of the junior program to which the Committee pays tribute. We agree with the Committee that the time to teach our youth to shoot is before they don the military uniform; that we can do it infinitely better than the military and at an infinitely lower cost to the taxpayer. On the other hand, methinks the Committee was engaged in a bit of double-talk. It denied our request to increase appropriation by $80,000 for the procurement of the ten rounds of .22 caliber ammunition necessary to support the program during this fiscal year and in lieu thereof substituted the language quoted above. If the National Board should divert $80,000 out of the $100,000 appropriated, as suggested, it could provide the junior clubs with bullets, but it is obvious that it would destroy itself in the process. The report continues: "The senior rifle clubs, deprived of a partial potential membership by the Selective Service Act, are more and more concerned of the 'hobby shooters,' generally older persons, and more to provide their own necessities. Services for this older age group may well be abandoned in favor of concentration on the age group 12 to 18 years wherein basic elements of the handling of arms must still be taught." Here is misinformation and lack of understanding compounded. The Selective Service, far from depriving the senior rifle clubs a partial potential membership, should be their strongest recruiting agency. The ability to shoot well cannot be acquired in the few short hours devoted to marksmanship training in the recruit depots of the Regular Services. It takes many years of practice to make a good shot. It requires continuous persistent practice thereafter to retain proficiency. The man who would benefit most from a well-rounded and universal civilian marksmanship training program is the one who has completed the required service in uniform, and who is eligible for recall duty at any time during his years as a Reserve thereafter. It is the most critical period for these men of military age. Congress would deny them the opportunity to retain the asset most valuable to them in time of war - the ability to use their personal weapons. The success of the junior program which the Committee reports depends entirely upon the ability and enthusiasm of the "older group" and "hobby shooter" whom the Committee belittles. It is they who are the bone and sinew of the civilian marksmanship program. If it is a "hobby" to give of ones time, money and services in the interests of the national defense, Congress would be well advised to encourage such a hobby to fullest extent rather than to deny it the means of sustenance. It is my belief that the Committee was influenced in its remarks bv those who should be the strongest supporters of the National Board program but who are too blind to recognize its potential. I refer, of course, to those who believe that the military can teach our youth the rudiments of marksmanship. While giving lip service to the National Board, there it evidence that they speak of it in disparaging terms in the interactive sessions of the Congressional Committees on Appropriations and Armed Services. The record, however, does not support their point of view. The records of World War II and Korea are proof enough that the military's inability to provide adequate marksmanship training for our armed forces. If they would seek out the truth they would find that their best marksmen and many of their leaders are the products of the civilian marksmanship to program. If they were entirely honest and unbiased, they would have to admit that it is the "hobby shooter" to whom  they should turn for instructors and advice in the marksmanship field during a major mobilization. It is high time that the Members of Congress should listen to their civilian constituents in this matter, rather than to the men in uniform who have so singularly failed in the teaching of basic marksmanship and the ability to hit what is aimed at. It is the fundamental point in the making of General Hodge's infantryman. The NRA and the National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice stand ready and willing to do their part, if only Congress will give them the wherewithal to function efficiently and effectively.

A push for United Nations action on global gun bans - expected in July - has been preceded with release of a worldwide propaganda video that paints its message blood red, and I quote: "A gun born ... a killer is on the loose ... small arms are not fussy about the company they keep ... and they can murder indiscriminately." This film - "Armed to the Teeth: The Worldwide Plague of Small Arms" - is a prelude to a UN conference on a global gun control scheme that could deeply affect Americans' future right to keep and bear arms. "The United Nations Conference on the Illicit Trade in Small Arms and All Its Aspects" will be held in July at UN headquarters in New York. On its face, this sounds like an effort to target rogue gunrunners and terrorists, but only in part. And therein is the trap. Opposition to the UN summit will be smeared as support for international crime. That would be a lie. Our opposition stems from something that should be dear to all Americans - our national sovereignty and individual Freedom. This summer's conference culminates years of work by a host of leftist groups, many working under the direction of something called the International Action Network on Small Arms (IANSA) and the UN Preparatory Committee (PrepCom), which met this past January and published a manifesto they hope will override our Bill of Rights. It is called the "Draft Programme of Action ...." In its foggy dialectic, "illicit" doesn't mean what a reasonable person might think it means. In their translation, your guns and my guns are also ultimately "illicit" guns. Further, "All Its Aspects" also covers legal commerce in firearms, and legal private ownership. Among those associated with and supporting IANSA's worldwide gun ban efforts are: Coalition for Gun Control, Canada; Coalition for Gun Control, New Zealand; Coalition to Stop Gun Violence, USA; Million Mom March, USA; and National Coalition for Gun Control, Australia. All of these groups are pressing for worldwide gun control measures that include international firearms registration and primacy of the "world criminal court" over violations. The IANSA lists among its major funding sources: the Ford Foundation, the Rockefeller Foundation, Ploughshears Fund, The Compton Foundation, Belgian Ministry for Development Cooperation, Swedish Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the United Kingdom Department for International Development. Virtually alone against this array of richly funded international pressure groups is the NRA. The Bulletin of Atomic Scientists advises, "If activists want to fight the NRA and like-minded groups on the international level, they must confront them at home, because domestic and international weapons issues are intertwined." Anyone who would argue that this international battle is only about terrorists and illegal guns need only look at what the global gun control forces are saying. In a summation of a pre-conference planning session in January, IANSA reported, "The speakers urged the Conference to take action in key areas affecting both the legal and illegal trade including ... controls on the availability, use and storage of small arms within states, including strong domestic firearms regulation as well as a prohibition on the sale and possession of military weapons by civilians." And in their view, any firearm ever used by any armed forces or based on military design is a "military" weapon. The end game which includes the aggressive use of "transnational" power - thus overriding national sovereignty regarding firearms - is the collection and destruction of firearms, including guns from what they condescendingly call in UN bureaucratese "civil society."
