From the standpoint of both attendance and interest, this year's meetings established a new high since the halcyon days of 1930. More Directors were in attendance than at any other time during the past five years, and one hundred and five Directors and members sat down at the informal dinner which closed the meetings. General A. B. Critchfield, the man who created Camp Perry out of the mud flats on the shores of Lake Erie, was elected President of the Association. On the following day he enlisted support of important members of Congress and the military establishment in a plan which, if successful, will straighten the entire firing line at Camp Perry by removing the unused buildings in Erie Proving Ground which now cause the small-bore range, running-deer range, and police-practice ranges to be separated from the main firing line. Plans are already under discussion with the necessary authorities in the War Department for the expansion of the small-bore range to double its present facilities, and for the installation of two running-deer targets in place of the one now on the range. Funds for the National Matches are assured in the War Department Bill which was reported to Congress on the Monday following the N.R.A. meetings. There were authorized changes in the small-bore regulations which will materially speed-up tournaments at Camp Perry, as well as all tournaments throughout the country; and a new design of target rack has been worked out at Headquarters which will still further speed-up operations on small-bore ranges at Perry and elsewhere. The Executive Officers of the Association have been instructed by the Executive Committee to cooperate with the War Department in an effort to hold the National Matches not later than the last two weeks in August and the first week in September. This will not only insure better weather, but will make it much easier to fit the School of Instruction and N.R.A. Matches into the August vacation of many shooters. The officers of the Association will also cooperate with the Director of Civilian Marksmanship in endeavoring to work out an improved set of regulations for the issuance of equipment to both Junior and Senior N.R.A. clubs. Meanwhile we are informed that the Navy plans to return to the lists with a National Match Team in 1936. With the stimulus provided by these activities, .30-caliber shooting will unquestionably reach a new peak this year. The Executive Committee also approved sending a small-bore team to England in 1937, in an effort to recapture the Pershing Trophy. A system of registered tournaments, beginning with the St. Petersburg Shoot at Florida-March Sth to 8th inclusive, will be used as an important part of the plan for selecting this International Team. It will not be necessary to depend upon Postal Matches, or a single try-out at Camp Perry or elsewhere. Every competitor who takes part in a registered shoot during 1936 and early 1937 will place himself in a position to be considered for the 1937 team that goes to England. The effect of this plan in stimulating interest in properly supervised small-bore shooting should be enormous. Certainly the shooting game has set its sights for a new record score in 1936. The sportsmanlike cooperation of all shooters with one another and their local clubs, and the active support of individuals and clubs of the National Association, will insure progress for the game during the year ahead, far beyond anything heretofore thought possible.

In 1871 the National Rifle Association of America was founded by a small group of National Guard officers in the State of New York for the purpose of improving its members in marksmanship. From that hopeful beginning it has developed into a nation-wide, nonprofit, membership organization of more than a quarter million members. Its objects are "to promote social welfare and public safety, law and order, and the national defense; to educate and train citizens of good repute in the safe and efficient handling of small arms, and in the technique of design, production and group instruction; to increase the knowledge of small arms and promote efficiency in the use of such arms on the part of members of law enforcement agencies, of the armed forces and of citizens who would be subject to service in the event of war; and generally to encourage the lawful ownership and use of small arms by citizens of good repute". Work has started on a new Headquarters Building for the National Rifle Association in Washington. The one and-a-half-million-dollar service center for the shooters of America will replace a group of four assorted buildings into which the NRA has expanded during the past 17 years. This new building will make possible more efficient services to its members and will provide facilities for an expanded program of public service. Every building of lasting significance is a symbol of an ideal - our magnificent cathedrals are a symbol to our faith in God; our many schools and universities are  symbol of our belief in education. They are everlasting monuments in our community living. Likewise, our new modern NRA Headquarters Building will be a symbol of our contribution to the American way of life. Because we believe in the right of loyal American citizens to own and use firearms for lawful purposes; because we believe in firearms safety education; be cause we believe in marksmanship training; because we believe in shooting for sport; here is an opportunity to enlarge our vision. Because of these beliefs we are on the threshold of growth and national greatness. In striving to reach our ideal we open the door of opportunity for public service to this generation of American citizens and those to follow. It has been the unselfish action of our members and friends, growing slowly into the habit of devotion, and in many cases into a sort of consecration, that has made possible the NRA of today. We are now on this threshold of a new era. By the grace of God and with the wholehearted cooperation of all of us who believe that guns and shooting are a vital part of the United States of America, this NRA Headquarters Building will surely become the symbol of our ideal.

ALL of us fighting to defend our rights learned long ago that there will never be time to rest. As soon as we get one anti-gun crisis contained, it seems to re-appear in another form. That's what we're seeing with so-called "cop killer bullets." Let's get one thing straight: The real problem is "cop killer criminals," most of whom have a long record of lenient treatment by the "justice system" before they killed a cop. Even today, almost 15 years after the media created the "cop killer bullet" issue, there has never been a police officer killed by the penetration of Kevlar body armor by a bullet designed for that purpose. In 1966, three law enforcement professionals designed a bullet specifically for police use, called the KTW (from the three men's initials). Its metal composition and Teflon coating (largely added to protect the gun's barrel) allowed police to penetrate car doors in gunfights with criminals. Minimal quantities were quietly produced, which served well and without incident for over a decade. But in late 1981, NBC exposed KTW with a hysterical prime-time TV segment entitled "Cop Killer Bullets" in which they shot a KTW bullet through police body armor draped on a mannequin.	Law enforcement officials pleaded with NBC not to air this "how-to" for criminals, fearing they'd seek out the unknown ammunition or target the more vulnerable body areas of police officers. Yet NBC defied them and, incredibly, aired the segment again six months later. CBS, ABC and print media picked up the issue and the "cop killer bullet" scandal was born. Media-hungry politicians quickly introduced a bill to prohibit manufacture of any bullet capable of penetrating a Kevlar vest. It was so broadly written it would have banned almost all hunting rifle ammunition. Even the U.S. Treasury and Justice Departments called the ban "flawed" and "unworkable" because it would "invariably include a wide range of ammunition commonly used for hunting, target shooting or other legitimate and long-established [defensive and] sporting purposes." In 1986, Congress enacted a bill that banned production and importation of bullets composed of certain hard metals intended for penetration of light metal or body armor. Even the original bill's author. Rep. Mario Biaggi said, "Our final legislative product was not some watered down version of what we set out to do. In the end, there was no compromise on the part of police safety." Because no law officer has been killed by a so-called "cop-killer" bullet penetrating his or her body armor since the law went into effect, Congress and the news media thought they had accomplished something important. But remember, no officer had been killed by penetration of a vest before the law went into effect. However, thanks to the media's reckless exposure of information about bullet-resistant vests - which were still largely unheard of - criminals learned to shoot police in the head, neck and other exposed areas, and have admitted deliberately doing so. After Congress passed the so-called "cop-killer bullet" bill, the controversy settled down. And it should have stayed down. But in the wake of the Oklahoma City bombing, President Bill Clinton and anti-gun Rep. Charles Schumer decided to resurrect the "cop killer bullet" scam, milk it for all the headlines it was worth, and then use it to once again attack legal firearm and ammunition ownership. When the House Judiciary Committee was considering H.R. 1710, the anti-terrorism bill, Rep. Schumer tried to tack on an amendment that would give the attorney general and the Administration authority to ban any bullet that they claimed met met criteria that they alone would interpret; in other words, since they could make up the rules as they went along, they could ban anything they wanted. So "cop-killer" is just a stalking horse - a sneaky way to ban conventional, everyday ammunition. The Department of Justice said a ban like Schumer's "would effectively deprive firearm owners of the use of their weapons by rendering illegal all available ammunition." As for President Clinton's proposal, it could ban the .30-30 Winchester, .30-06 Springfield, .308 Winchester, .270 Winchester, .243 Winchester, .223 Remington, .375 Magnum, .44 Magnum and virtually every other rifle or high-powered pistol cartridge. By forcing gun owners into defending what he brands "cop-killer" ammunition, Clinton clearly plans to discredit gun owners and smear the NRA. And by banning the ammunition, he can literally take the bang out of the right to bear arms, without ever touching firearms themselves. Schumer's deceptive attack on our rights is also still underway, and we must be ready to fight it when the time comes - when he offers it as an amendment to the anti-terrorism bill or something else. Nobody, and this goes double for the nation's firearms owners, wants law enforcement officers hurt. Working together, we can replace anti-gun emotion with these facts: Right now, six levels of protective vests are available to law enforcement officers. According to the leading vest manufacturer, the chance of police encountering handgun ammunition capable of defeating commonly worn vests is "remote." Neither before nor since 1986, when Congress passed the federal law restricting KTW and similar rounds to police, no police officer in the United States has been killed with any handgun bullet of this type fired through the protective material of a soft body vest. Contrary to inflammatory media reports, there have been no new developments in ammunition designed to penetrate body armor. The "Black Rhino" bullet was a hoax. And ABC's Nightline proved it. The real problem isn't ammunition - the problem is criminals. Individuals with prior criminal histories are involved in the majority of shootings that kill law enforcement officers. During the past 10 years, 73% had prior criminal arrests, and 23% were actually on parole or probation when officers were killed. These are the facts your congressmen and women most need to hear from you - RIGHT NOW. Call Congress: Tel. (202) 224-3121.

Some of my mail shows interest in the controversy, the distractions, going on in the NRA. A smattering of these letters demands to know what is going on. More of them deplore publishing the controversy and the distractions. Good members have read in some place about problems. They want to know the truth and I have no problem with that! So it has occurred to me that, as we go to our Annual Members' Meeting and our Board Meeting in Milwaukee in the last week of May, coming soon, and because this is the last issue of our magazine which you will see prior to your arrival there, (and there are those who hope this is the last they will see on this subject), I should use this page to give you certain unvarnished truths. During the past year, the membership of NRA has given overwhelming support to the objectives to which we are so properly dedicated. However, some of the letters, to which I referred above, reveal misunderstandings - even distortions - of the facts. Some of these distortions have been irresponsibly and shamelessly published. We are approaching 2,900,000 members, and we are going on shortly to 3,000,000. This is evidence of the faith which the American people have in the National Rifle Association. And retaining that faith, we shall go on growing in numbers and in effectiveness until, finally, no political leader in America, mindful of his future, will carelessly or recklessly confront us on the right of Law-abiding and decent people to keep and bear arms. ILA has been standing tall and dedicated. Let's get it straight, of course, there's been a lot of debate and there's nothing wrong with that. A few good and well-intentioned members of NRA have been confused by reports of fears - fears that were not and never shall become, reality. Some of that has been based on honest misunderstandings and some of it based on deliberate distortions heralded by dissidents. ILA's position has not changed, and, indeed, is not going to change when examined by the sound and enduring principles existing when we face the gun control issue. It is simple. When we are on the defense, we yield nothing. We never back down. We never give an inch. When we are on the offense, we take all we can get - all the reforms, all the improvements, that we can get, This is honest. It possesses now, and will continue to possess, an easily understood and historical virtue. That is it. Nothing more. However, the statement has been made and published that NRA would "gut the McClure/Volkmer bill. S 914, and that the NRA would support gun registration." Those are absolutely vile and unprincipled falsehoods. And I can prove it by the official United States Senate transcript of proceedings of the hearings on S 914, at which Warren Cassidy, the Executive Director of ILA, testified. Cassidy testified in support of S 914 as accepted and supported by Senator James A. McClure and Congressman Harold L. Volkmcr When Cassidy's prepared statement had been finished, he was asked by the Chairman whether NRA would support certain changes. Cassidy replied simply and directly that changes were acceptable, provided they did not take the core of our position out of the bill; that is, that the changes would not gut S 914 as supported by Senator McClure. Time passed, and on March 12, 1984, Cassidy and I met with Senator McClure and members of his staff to discuss the bill. We agreed, clearly and firmly: first, that NRA supported and would support S 914, unamended, as supported by Senator McClure; second, that if that should fade, NRA would join Senator McClure in his support of a further refinement supported by the Administration and by Senator Hatch, who is also hard and straight on our issue. Again, on March 22, 1984, we met with Senator McClure and his staff to assure unity in our efforts, to put the seal of NRA's agreement, to join Senator McClure in an amendment agreeable to Senator McClure, and only provided it were agreeable to Senator McClure. In the Senate, it is McClure's bill. Now I have a question: if those people who have aroused suspicions, misunderstandings and distortions as to NRA's position do not trust Senator McClure with his own bill and NRA's support of it, whom do they trust? And then come the nasty accusations with anti-Semitics overtones that NRA has joined up with the Anti Defamation League of B'nai B'rith in a scheme to stop or to limit firearms training in America. That is an accusation so outrageously asinine and so perfidiously conceived as to tempt a reasonable man to ignore it. But it has now been published and repeated too often to be ignored. It was published that the NRA and the ADL teamed up to pass some restraint im West Virginia - a total and absolute falsehood. NRA opposed the paramilitary bill in West Virginia and we had an NRA field representative in that state capitol for five days working to assure that it would not pass. It did not pass. But something did come out of this, which shortsighted people ignore, but which they should appreciate. The ADL, knowing the NRA does not support their bill, accepted our amendment to protect our members' rights. So far as I know, this is the first time the ADL has indicated agreement that there is an individual right to keep and bear arms. These are straight, hard, provable facts concerning NRA as we go to Milwaukee for our Annual Meetings. I hope you will be there, all of you who can, 2,900,000 strong. Keep NRA growing. Keep NRA united and strong.

In the early history of our country a major part of an American boy's education was devoted to the use of the hoe, the ax, and the rifle. These were required subjects even if he had little opportunity to learn the three R's of formal education. Most of his learning was acquired from the experiences of everyday living. The change in the mode of living in our society and the ever-increasing availability of leisure time have created a need for outdoor experiences, an understanding of physical environment, and the wise use of natural resources. Schools and colleges have a responsibility for teaching outdoor skills, appreciations, and attitudes for outdoor living if the wise use of leisure time is to be achieved and if people are to receive maximum satisfactions in outdoor activities. Today, outdoor education is the concern of the whole educational program. These subjects must be taught to our youth, not as an essential knowledge for survival, but as an experience in wholesome lifetime pursuits. Baseball, basketball, and football have been part of our educational program for many years. These activities tend to become spectator sports where the entertainment is great but the physical development benefits are confined to a relatively few skilled players. Participation is limited to a few years even for those who excel. Professional educators in the physical education field have been concerned for some time over the lack of emphasis on activities that have lifetime value for all the people. Prominent among these are outdoor pursuits such as shooting, hunting, casting, fishing, and other outdoor activities which have significant implications for the conservation of human and natural resources. Some few schools have instituted courses in outdoor education to teach students the basic skills in these activities which give pleasure to so many millions. The time is ripe for further action on a national scale. The American Association for Health, Physical Education and Recreation (a department of the National Education Association) has taken the initiative by holding several exploratory meetings with other people interested in these activities. A survey was made of more than 6000 high schools and 533 colleges. This showed that over 12 percent of the schools and 21 percent of the colleges already had programs including fishing or shooting or both, while 55 percent of the schools and 47 percent of the colleges said they were interested in instituting such programs. The Outdoor Education Project was the result. This five-year project follows the successful plan of cooperation of business, industry, and education. Funds have been provided by the Associated Fishing Tackle Manufacturers and the Sporting Arms and Ammunition Manufacturers' Institute. Leadership training, interpretation of the program to school administrative officials, program development, and the preparation of materials are aims of the project. The American Association for Health, Physical Education and Recreation, working with other departments of the National Education Association, the National Rifle Association of America, and the industries involved, will carry forward the project to speed the development of outdoor education programs. Through nine regional and state workshops held in 1956, a total of 933 educational leaders was brought into close contact with this program. Fifteen additional workshops are being scheduled for future months. Others are on a waiting list. At these workshops qualified instructors from industry and the National Rifle Association assist in a program designed to prepare selected people in the educational field to establish and conduct outdoor education in their own schools. The National Rifle Association of America believes in the Outdoor Education Project and has participated in all phases of the program. NRA members and other sportsmen should be acquainted with this development. Although there is little fanfare connected with it, outdoor education offers a splendid opportunity for qualified sportsmen to render significant public service which will promote the sport of shooting and benefit the whole community. Many local schools will welcome an offer to help. Those of us who love guns and shooting should encourage and assist our educators in their efforts to include safe and efficient gun handling in outdoor education.

These words were written just after the last shots were fired in competition at the 1992 Olympic Games. For many, the Summer Games mark the end of year - of training and preparation. I see them as a new beginning for NRA as the National Governing Body for the shooting sports, and the start of a new era of excellence for the U.S. Shooting Team. There are those who refuse to recognize our shoot accomplishments, who choose to criticize or ignore them. The lack of coverage of the Olympic shooting events by NBC is a travesty we will remember. But we face the future with confidence. And this confidence is underscored by shooters like Launi Meili. She brought home an Olympic gold medal in smallbore rifle from Barcelona at age 29. Launi exemplifies the dedication that earns the ultimate reward and makes her a role model for the growing number of women competitors. Bob Poth, who won a silver medal, gave up his job as a teacher to become a world class shooter. He, too, deserves the admiration of every American. But what of the other shooters who make many sacrifices to win in international competition? Who will them with leadership, training and financial assistance to help them become Olympic champions? The answer is NRA. Never before have we been more committed to their future success. At the request of the U.S. Olympic Committee, NRA was asked to review the various procedures we employed to carry out our responsibilities as the National Governing Body for the shooting sports and to make adjustments that would bring the Association into full compliance under the USOC Constitution. We formed a special committee to make recommendations that would satisfy the USOC request while allowing changes to be set in motion that would enhance the probability our shooters will achieve their goals. The findings of the committee led to important changes in our relationship with the team through the NRA International Competitions Committee. The character of the ICC and the NRA Bylaws were amended and unanimously approved by the NRA Board of Directors. Most of the changes are already in place. The ICC is more independent in its operation than ever before, and a majority of its members are elected by the athletes themselves. NRA now dedicates more resources to the program and has designed a new system of vertical shooter development to bring promising young international shooters through the development cycle much faster. But perhaps the single most important factor in this entire plan is the consolidation of all our efforts under the leadership of Gary Anderson. Gary is one of the most respected international shooters of all time. He won two Olympic gold medals and seven world championships. It is very apparent that he is the single most qualified person in the nation to provide the direction and inspiration our young shooters need to succeed. In his new position as executive director of International Shooting Sports, Gary Anderson's sole task is to build a shooting team that is second to none in Olympic-style competition. Managing the day-to-day operations of the US Shooting Team and implementing its complex training program is Lones Wigger. A legend in his own right, Lones earned two gold and one silver medal during his years on the ranges of the Olympic Games. He's also been a smallbore rifle national champion more times than there is space here to list, including another record-setting performance on the firing lines of the National Matches in July. Lones has even arranged for the U.S. Olympic Shooting Center to become part of the NRA member recruitment program. There has been a tremendous amount of time and hard work put in at every level of NRA to ensure the success of this new program for the team. There have also been detractors. But we have sen obscure, petty groups before that have tried to hide a self-serving agenda under the cloak of righteous indignation. In the end, they do little more than demonstrate they know nothing of what the real shooting fraternity is all about. In this case, common sense prevailed once again. Our proposed changes were submitted to the USOC Membership Committee in June. The committee voted unanimously to accept them with a few minor changes and endorse the Association as the National Governing Body for the shooting sports. A full vote by the NRA Board of Directors and USOC this fall with complete the formalities. The leadship and financial commitment are in place to develop the U.S. Shooting Team into a world leader in every discipline. In 1992 alone, NRA has pledged $1.2 million in direct support, $800,000 in like services and it will continue to be instrumental in raising $200,000 through International Shooter Development Fund. All of this support goes directly to our team. The U.S. Shooting Team is an integral part of international competition and the Olympic Games. To the over 18 million Americans who target shoot each, the team and its members are a constant reminder of true sportsmanship. They join other NRA programs in such areas as hunting, firearms safety, instructor certification and other forms of competitive shooting as examples of what it means to be part of the family of 70 million law-abiding gun owners throughout our nation. As your executive vice president, I pledge that NRA will expand its leadership position in all the shooting sports. And I assure you this is just the beginning.

If that small group of men who banded together to form the National Rifle Association a little more than eighty years ago had chosen a motto for their newly formed organization, without doubt they would have selected the Second Article of the Bill of Rights. Certainly there could be no better expression of our basic objectives than those words which read "A well regulated militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed." If we stop to analyze it we find within that sentence the major objectives for which the NRA stands today. The first, and the one which most frequently comes to mind, is the phrase "to keep." These words are the rallying cry for the continuous fight we wage against those laws, ordinances and regulations which would deny the rights of law-abiding citizens to purchase and to keep rifles, handguns and shotguns in their possession so long as they use them only for lawful purposes. Closely associated with the phrase "to keep" is the one "to bear." The two go hand in hand. The right to own a personal weapon amounts to little without the corresponding right to carry it from place to place - from home to range, from tournament to tournament, in the upland country in the search for birds, or in the deepest wilds in the hunt for game. It makes no difference so long as the carrying and the use of the weapons are for a lawful purpose. The majority of our members think of the right to keep and bear arms in connection with their recreation. Although the drafters of the Bill of Rights may have envisioned the regulatory laws that are proposed so frequently today, this Article was not adopted for such a purpose alone. There were the questions of a well regulated militia and the security of a free State as well as the individual rights of law-abiding citizens within the Republic to be considered. The value of the militia - the great mass of potential soldiers - is determined by how well it is regulated. The same truth applies to our Regular forces. Both must be well regulated - well trained - if they are to play an effective part in the national defense. We find this principle in the original charter of the NRA which sets forth its purposes "to improve its members in marksmanship and to promote a system of aiming drill and rifle practice as a part of the military drill of the National Guard of the various States." It was this principle which brought the National Board for Promotion of Rifle Practice into being in 1903. Congress did not set up that agency just to give away free ammunition or to provide a means for NRA Members to purchase obsolescent rifles. Congress, instead, had in mind the creation of a great civilian reservoir of trained marksmen for the express purpose of furthering the security of our State. In seeking a civilian organization qualified to teach other civilians of military age how to hit a mark. Congress singled out the NRA as the one which alone had the knowledge and the ability to do so. In the light of our experience we firmly believe that the National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice does fill an important niche in the defense of our country. Because of this belief we urged the 82nd Congress to appropriate sufficient funds to continue its functions for the next fiscal year. If we expect Congress to add to these Appropriations in the future, if we expect that the broad objectives of the National Board are ever to be attained, then we as an Association have an obligation to perform. We must see to it that the rifles we draw, the Government ammunition we receive or purchase, and the range equipment we borrow, are used for the purposes for which they are intended. We must redouble our efforts to train the youth of the country in marksmanship and to carry out the task assigned to us by the federal statutes pertaining to the "Promotion of Rifle Practice." The training of free men in the use of small arms is a primary mission of our Association. Surely the right of the people to keep and bear arms carries with it the obligation to be prepared to use them in the security of the State.

The 1968 Federal Gun Control Law requires personal identification from buyers of firearms and ammunition, with certain exceptions. Form 4473, covering the sale of firearms by licensed dealers, asks for "Type of Identification (Driver's License, etc.)" and, next question, "Number on Identification." It indicates that identification other than driver's licenses is acceptable. On handgun and .22 rimfire ammunition sales, every licensed dealer must maintain a "bound book" showing "the method used by the licensee to establish the identity of the purchaser (transferee)." The last column provides for an entry revealing whether identification is by driver's license or "Other - specify." While identification usually has taken the form of a driver's license, then, it certainly is not confined to that. We therefore would like to make a helpful suggestion - helpful to all those concerned with opposing anti-gun laws and with organizing support for that purpose. Instead of showing your driver's license, show your voter registration card if you live in a State that issues them. The dealer who records your gun or ammunition purchase will note on his records that you are a registered voter. This can be significant and indeed important. For any local organization seeking to defeat anti-gun laws and their supporters can then, with the dealer's permission, make a quick, handy and up-to-date list of registered voters who might be inclined to oppose anti-gun moves. The result, in fact, would be the most complete and current list possible of firearms owners who might be expected to vote in support of the right to bear arms. According to sound legal authority, there is no reason why any group or individual cannot compile such a list. Dealer records, while required by law, are the physical property of the dealer himself. Under the Gun Control Law, they must be kept on his premises for inspection by IRS agents at any time. But if he chooses to open his records to anyone for any purpose, there is not a word in the law against it. So, if you want a list, get the names of firearms dealers in your area (they are available from telephone and city directories) and proceed from there. And meanwhile when you must identify yourself to buy firearms, or hand gun or .22 rimfire ammunition, show the man behind the counter your voter registration card. It is valid, beyond question, provided it bears a serial number and, in buying handguns and .22 rimfire ammunition, even if it lacks a number. Such action, simple as it is, could serve to impress the fact that many voters value the right to bear arms as highly as the right to vote.

Once each year, during the month of August, thousands of Americans attend 4 special courses of instruction in rifle and pistol marksmanship at Camp Perry, Ohio. The schools are sponsored by the National Board for the Promotion of Rifle Practice and the National Rifle Association of America to develop qualified instructors who will train our citizens in the proper and efficient handling of small arms. They are open to individuals, both military and civilian, who are 14 years of age or older. The mission of the Small Arms Firing Schools for rifle and pistol is to bring to civilians and to members of the various components of the Armed Forces, not reached through training programs conducted within the active military service, information concerning the most modern methods of marksmanship instruction in order to raise the standards of performance in the use of individual military arms by the citizens of our country. Each school consists of 3 courses - regular, special, and coaches. The regular course is planned for new or less-experienced shooters and is designed to teach correct shooting fundamentals to beginners and to improve the shooting skills of others. The special course is planned for experienced shooters and is designed to produce qualified marksmanship instructors as well as to improve the shooting skills of the student. The coaches course is planned for 'master' shooters and instructors and is designed to provide practical experience in coaching and improving the skills of less proficient shooters. Students attending the rifle school fire the Service rifle and those attending the pistol school fire the Service pistol, except beginners who fire the cal. .22 pistol. Instructors are specially selected individuals from the U.S. Army Marksmanship Training Unit and the Weapons Dept, of the U. S. Army Infantry School at Ft. Benning, Ga. The purpose of the Police Marksmanship School is to present specialized up-to-date techniques of law-enforcement tactics involving the use of firearms. The school provides law-enforcement personnel with a place to discuss methods of training and to fire marksmanship training courses. It affords an opportunity for police organizations to send representatives who will be qualified, upon successful completion of the course, to establish or improve law-enforcement training programs in local communities. Instructors are selected from the Armed Forces, governmental agencies, and police departments for their outstanding ability in a particular phase of police instruction. They are changed from year to year to provide different views on training and methods used. Adults who attend the NRA Instructor-Junior School receive, during the first 2 days, information on fundamentals of instruction, how to teach rifle marksmanship, club organization, and NRA shooting programs. For the next 4 days they receive practical experience in teaching basic fundamentals of marksmanship and match firing to students using cal. .22 rifles or air guns. Instructors are individual NRA members who serve without compensation, assisted in their job by selected marksmanship instructors and coaches of the U.S. Marine Corps. The significance of the Camp Perry Marksmanship Schools is indicated by the fact that total attendance for the 4 schools in 1963 was in excess of 6000 students. Their value to the defense of our country will be reflected as these qualified people return to their military units and civilian shooting organizations to encourage shooting and to teach marksmanship to others. A prepared citizenry, trained to do a soldier's job with a soldier's skill when necessity calls, is essential to a strong America. Marksmanship training in time of peace is vital to individual preparedness in case of war. Our national defense effort receives a real contribution from the Camp Perry Marksmanship Schools.

Last year, for better or worse, the American people accepted a staggering responsibility. In different quarters it was called many things: The Marshall plan. The Russian problem. National defense. The atomic bomb. Balance of power. Hemisphere solidarity. And, as always, there was a price to pay. The figures grew ominously. U.S. plans for a better world were going to cost more dollars than any of us thought existed. But behind all of the names, in all of the guises, and back of the price tag lay one inevitable, inescapable fact. The American people had accepted the responsibility of world leadership. Perhaps "accepted" is too strong a word. Most Americans, even after an uneasy year of looking squarely at the thing, have not put the jigsaw together. In too many minds America's plans and problems are still just plans and problems, and not separate aspects of a fateful destiny that lies ahead. Those labels, those price tags and headaches, and those responsibilities are part and parcel of our leadership. They are inevitable. America can no more abandon her position, her stature, her responsibilities, or her grasp on the reins of a shaky-world than could England have ignored her position after the defeat of the Spanish Armada. We alone among nations have survived two wars to emerge as the one powerful and genuinely peace-loving country in the world. The implication of that fateful evolution among nations puts a Herculean task squarely before the American people. Living up to the greatest challenge ever handed a nation means that we, as individuals, are going to have to learn to think BIG. Big and clearly. Here is a sample of the kind of big thinking that must come from Americans this year: Congress, almost certainly, will pass some kind of Marshall plan for the economic relief of Europe. Looking at it coldly, that relief is a selfishly-dictated policy which will strengthen America's position in world affairs. BUT, the astronomical amount which even a modified Marshall plan will entail is only a fraction of the story. President Truman's Air Policy Commission recommends, by 1952, the annual expenditure of nearly twenty billion dollars for armed defense - mainly toward the creation of an adequate air force. And there is universal military training to consider. This is where the thinking comes in. There is a growing feeling in some quarters that we must have an enormously strengthened defense structure first, in order to provide the sense of security in which a Marshall plan can function. Others would have us subordinate the Marshall plan entirely. The defense machine envisioned by the President's advisors, they say, backed by a system of universal military training, plus guarantees to certain key European countries, would be more effective in bringing about economic (and eventually, political) recovery in Europe than a full Marshall plan. From these alternatives a choice must be made. That choice should be a reflection of the considered opinion of the majority of the American people. When we have that, we will have won the first round in a personal realization of our position among nations. Our prime obligation is to assume real, thinking leadership. To do so, questions like these must be answered in the mind of every American. We must think big, and clearly, and see the world as it is, and ourselves as a part of it. This year, perhaps more than any in the history of our country, is the year of decision. If we can think big enough as individuals, 1948 may yet see the creation of tools by which we can forge the structure of a peaceful, balanced world.

On occasion I have been asked how NRA's election process works, is the method accurate and foolproof as possible, and could it he improved. During the September NRA Board Meetings your Directors were addressed by Mr. Nile J. Webb, CPA, a partner in the nationally known firm of Deloitte Haskins & Sells, and an accountant for 31 years. In response to questions about the accuracy of our ballot counting procedure and its universally accepted standards, Mr. Webb stated that not only was NRA's management and its election committee "super careful" in obtaining the most accurate count possible but the extra program steps we include go far beyond the normal counting procedure. No other system of which he is aware would significantly improve our present high degree of accuracy. The last step in the election process is the appointment of the Committee on Elections by the NRA President. This committee responsible for the conduct of elections selects an internationally known independent accounting firm to maintain proper control over the election of Directors and any amendments to the NRA Bylaws. They determine the validity of the ballots while monitoring ballot tabulation to assure accuracy and security. The firm oversees the entire system used to mail, receive and validate the ballots and they design, test and oversee the data entry system used to tabulate all votes. The process begins with the Committee on Elections determining the layout of the ballot, the order of names on the ballot and the number of different ballots to be printed. When listing the names in random order the accounting firm furnishes the random list of numbers that determines the order of names. In this manner, when the names are rotated and multiple ballots are printed in equal numbers, each nominee will be listed in various positions on the ballots. In the past 10 years, five rotating ballots per year have been printed. This printing of different ballots is done to give all the nominees an equal chance of being elected irrespective of alphabetical order. The ballots ate printed by an outside firm specializing in this type of printing. A unique number printed at the top of each ballot enables the accounting	firm to audit and account for all ballots, allows the detection of a duplicate ballot, keys the data entry system to the name rotation of that specific ballot. The number is in no way traceable to the identity of an individual voting member. After printing, the ballots are shipped to the magazine printing company, stored in a secured area for auditing by the accounting firm under controls established by the firm, the ballot issues go through the complete binding operation and are turned over for mailing to the U.S. Post Office (located in the plant). All leftover ballots are stored securely until destroyed. The final mailing of the ballot to those who don't receive a magazine, or who become voting members after the ballot magazine issue has been mailed is by first class mail. This mailing, like the mailing of the ballot magazine, is done under the control of the accountants who continually test the system to be sure that all voting members are being sent a ballot. All ballots are returned to the accounting firm's post office box, opened by the firm in its offices, batched for control, and placed in a special log. Batches are then brought to NRA data entry in locked cases to be keypunched into the data entry system. Each ballot is keypunched by two different operators with an auditor from the accounting firm making the final decision If there is a difference between the two totals. A percentage of the ballots in each batch is tested by the auditors to determine if the votes were keyed without error. When a batch has been correctly entered, the totals are released to the main count by a special code known only to the accounting firm's auditors. The batches of ballots are then returned to the accounting firm in locked cases. All ballots and envelopes must be held for 120 days after the election. Before the count is finalized numerous tests are performed by the auditors. When completed, the auditors report is prepared for NRA. All nominees are notified, and a report is prepared by the Committee on Elections for presentation at the next Annual Meeting of Members. What this rather technical explanation is meant to convey is this: NRA uses the most modern, accurate, confidential system available to count members' votes, whether for Directors elections or by laws amendments. Each and every member can be assured that his/her vote is included in the final total and is done so under the complete control of a responsible firm of unimpeachable credentials. In summary, while business techniques and methods may be upgraded as technology evolves, our time honored respect for the sanctity of the ballot box will never waiver.

IN Washington, D.C., hot and humid August is often the silly season. This year it was sillier than usual. Anti-gun U.S. Sen. Thomas J. Dodd, running for reelection in Connecticut as an "independent" after both major parties shunned him, asserted in The Congressional Record that this magazine had attempted to "intimidate" him with a form letter. He said that he refused to be intimidated. We are glad of that. No Senate page, much less a Senator, should be intimidated by a form letter. Senator Dodd also inserted in The Congressional Record (Aug. 17, 1970, pp. SI 3522-13523) a self-destructing statement that contained its own built-in denial of his claim that the 1968 Federal Gun Control Act is a success. He asserted that firearms arrests (not to be confused with convictions) under the act increased 313% over arrests under the previous Federal firearms laws. Included in what he inserted was a U.S. Treasury Department comment that the two sets of arrests were not statistically comparable, because the old law covered only nine kinds of violations whereas the 1968 act covers 26 possible violations. (And, we add, the enforcement'staff was doubled under the 1968 act, insuring more arrests of some kind or another.) An anonymous Pentagon spokesman, who preferred to remain anonymous for obvious reasons, made the remarkable admission, according to United Press International, that The National Rifle Association and its friends in Congress "pressured" the U.S. Army into lending support to the 40th World Shooting Championships at Phoenix in October. Scripps-Howard newspapers including the tabloid Washington Daily News then published an atrociously misleading cartoon by Basset on the subject. Apparently in an objection to humanitarianism, the cartoon totally ignored that much of the Army support consisted of physicians, medical corpsmen, ambulances and telephone service in case of illness or emergency among the thousands of competitors and spectators. Without a single corpse to show for it, FBI statisticians added 717 rural "murders" to the national total as if they actually occurred. The FBI Uniform Crime Report for 1969, released this August, listed 2,118 rural U.S. homicides although police reports gave only 1,401. As the reports covered only 75% of rural areas, the statisticians projected or assumed 717 homicides in the unreported areas - a much higher slaughter than the known murder rate. Anti-gun spokesmen naturally quote the inflated figure. Several other gun publications (but NOT The American Rifleman) published full-page paid advertisements by "Right To Bear Arms, Inc.," urging the election defeat of a yard-long list of Senators and Congressmen. Among those listed were some of the staunchest supporters of the right to bear arms, including U.S. Sens. Fannin (an NRA Member), Hruska and Murphy, and Reps. Casey (Tex.), McCulloch (Ohio) and others. Absurdly, the ad also called for the defeat in the Wisconsin Congressional election of Melvin Laird, who long ago left Congress and became Secretary of Defense. In a slippery piece of television "reporting," the Walter Cronkite CBS Evening News of Aug. 20 apparently blamed the jumbled full-page ad entirely on The American Rifleman and the NRA, neither of which had the least thing to do with it. A CBS "newsman" named David Schoumacher wrongly asserted that this magazine had "published a list of Congressmen supporting gun control, a clear signal to the hundreds of thousands of hunters who also happen to be voters." Trying to weasel out later, CBS claimed it referred to several items published 2 and a half to 20 months earlier - as far back as December, 1968, when there certainly was no election or question of influencing voters. U.S. Sen. Joseph D. Tydings, campaigning desperately for reelection in Maryland, also "made news" on CBS by proclaiming, on the strength of one California murder case allegedly involving a female Communist and three registered guns, that gun controls are anti-Communist rather than something favored by Communism. His remarks merely ignored world history. The Zodiac sign for most of August is Leo. But for some August goings-on, it ought to be a dunce cap.

As people do in the presence of death, we were reminiscing the other day . . . probing back into an almost forgotten time. We talked of the beginnings of the shooting game in America - the start of the "modern" era after World War I. We found it impossible to bring up any phase of the game as we know it that was not conceived or profoundly influenced by one man. In our time C. B. Lister has completely dominated one facet of the American scene. For three decades Lis served the cause of organized shooting in America with a singleness of purpose that might have stifled the thinking of a lesser man. For Lis it was broadening. It was devotion to a creative ideal - an ideal of freedom and lifelong devotion to something that he believed in deeply; that he wanted others to believe in. Lis's brand of patriotism was big and, as he liked to say, "practical". Marksmanship was patriotism to Lis. It meant more to him than a few people shooting at paper targets. For Lis the shooting game stood for sportsmanship and love of country. Characteristically, Lis was able to relate marksmanship to everything that was best in us. In so doing he made of it something that was bigger than it had ever been before. Lister's death is a shocking and tragic loss to the cause for which he did so much. He died at an age when most men can look forward to decades of useful living. Fortunately for the ideal to which Lis devoted his life, even the tragedy of his untimely death had its redeeming feature. Lis had something that most men are denied. He finished the job he set out to do. The legacy he leaves us is more than an organization called the National Rifle Association. Out of his clarity of vision, and the breadth of his approach, Lis gave us a way of thinking that will endure as long as our way of life endures. The legacy of C. B. Lister is the consciousness of a nation of free men of their right to bear arms.

The American people have a right to "keep and bear arms." This right is protected by the Second Amendment to the Constitution, just as the right to public editorial comment in this magazine is protected by the First Amendment. Americans remain committed to the constitutional right to free speech even when their most powerful times oracles have abused the First Amendment's inherent powers. Obviously the American people believe no democracy can survive without a free voice. In the same light, the authors of the Bill of Rights knew that a democratic republic has a right - indeed, a need - to keep and bear arms. Millions of American citizens just as adamantly believe the Second Amendment is crucial to the maintenance of the democratic process. Many express this belief through membership in the National Rifle Association of America. Our cause is neither trendy nor fashionable, but a basic American belief that spans generations. The NRA's strength has never originated in Washington but instead has reached outward and upward from Biloxi, Albuquerque, Concord, Tampa. Topeka - from every point on the compass and from communities large and small. Those who fail to grasp this widespread commitment will never understand the depth of political and philosophical dedication symbolized by the letters NRA. Scholars who have devoted careers to the study of the Second Amendment agree in principle that the right to keep and bear arms is fundamental to our concept of democracy. No high-court decision has yet found grounds to challenge this basic freedom. Yet some who oppose this freedom want to waive the constitutionality of the gun control question for the sake of their particular - and sometimes peculiar - brand of social reform. In doing so, they seem ready, even eager, to disregard a constitutional right exercised by at least 70 million Americans who own firearms. Contrary to current antigun evangelism, these gun owners are not bad people. They are hardworking, law abiding, tax paying. They are safe, sane and courteous in their use of guns. They have never been, nor will they ever be, a threat to law-and-order. history repeatedly warns us that human character cannot be scrubbed free of its defects through vain attempts to regulate inanimate objects such as guns. What has worked in the past, and what we see working now, are tough, NRA-supported measures that punish the incorrigible minority who place themselves outside the law. As a result of such measures, violent crimes with firearms, like assault and robbery, have stabilized or are actually declining. We see proof that levels of firearm ownership cannot be associated with levels of criminal violence, except for their deterrent value. On the other hand, tough laws designed to incarcerate violent offenders offer something gun control cannot: swift, sure justice meted out with no accompanying erosion of individual liberty. Violent crime continues to rise in New York and Washington, even after severe firearm control statutes were rushed into place. Criminals, understandably, have illegal ways of obtaining guns. Antigun laws - the waiting periods, background checks, handgun bans, et al - only harass those who obey them. Why should an honest citizen be deprived of a firearm for sport or self-defense when, for a gangster, obtaining a gun is just a matter of showing up on the right street corner with enough money? Antigun opinion steadfastly ignores these realities known to rank-and-file police officers - men and women who face crime firsthand, not administrators who face mayors and editors. These law enforcement professionals tell us that expecting firearm restrictions to act as crime-prevention measures is wishful thinking. They point out that proposed gun laws would not have stopped heinous crimes committed by the likes of John Hinckley, Jr, Patrick Purdy, Laurie Dunn or mentally disturbed, usually addicted killers. How can such crimes be used as examples of what gun control could prevent? There are better wavs to advance our society than to excuse criminal behavior. The NRA initiated the first hunter safety program, which has trained millions of young hunters. We are the shooting sports' leading safety organization with more than 26,000 certified instructors training 750,000 students and trainees last year alone. Through 1989 there were 9,818 NRA-certified law-enforcement instructors teaching marksmanship to thousands of peace officers. Frankly, we would rather keep investing NRA resources in such worthwhile efforts instead of spending our time and members' money debunking the failed and flawed promises of gun prohibitionists. If you agree, I invite you to join the NRA.

You were probably too busy at the time to pay much attention, but during the last war the NRA had a direct hand in teaching about one-and-three-quarter million Americans how to hit what they aimed at with a rifle. In the years from 1942 to 1945 the NRA's 4,000 senior rifle and pistol clubs were in a singularly opportune spot as far as marksmanship training was concerned. The nation needed small-arms instructors. The NRA had them. The nation needed equipment for small-arms training programs . . . films, printed instruction manuals, ranges on which classes could be conducted. The NRA had them, too . . . ready to go. Here are some figures that will give you an idea of the NRA's contribution, from the cancellation of the national rifle and pistol matches (1942) until VJ Day (1945): Pre-induction marksmanship training classes conducted by NRA club personnel: 2,862. Civilians trained in Army-approved basic small-arms firing: 158,956. NRA club-owned ranges made available for marksmanship training: 1,500. American communities involved: 1,278. The figures are even more impressive when they become a part of the enormous job done in small-arms training within the Armed Forces. Four hundred and fifty qualified small-arms instructors were commissioned from the NRA's membership rolls to conduct small-arms training programs in the armed services. These NRA members directly supervised the small-arms training of one-and-one third million officers and enlisted men of the United States Navy ... of more than a quarter million officers and enlisted men of the Army's service forces ... of 650,000 officers and men of the Air Forces . . . and of an undetermined number of officers and enlisted men of the United States Coast Guard. Total: Something in excess of one and three quarters million men. In addition . . . 500 civilian members of NRA rifle and pistol clubs served as foremen, inspectors, and toolmakers in small-arms and ammunition plants . . . 5,800 served as instructors in pre-induction marksmanship training classes throughout the country...125 pistolmen served as guards and instructors in plants . . . 2,450 civilian club members served as instructors, officers, or enlisted men of state guard, national guard, Coast Guard auxiliary and auxiliary police . . . and 250 of the NRA's handloaders turned 1,645,900 rounds of otherwise unobtainable ammunition for state guard units, police, and plant guards. In short, both the NRA and its affiliated clubs were ready and prepared to do a badly-needed job on short notice. That the NRA's wartime program played an important role in the nation's over all effort is attested by statements from President Truman, Generals Marshall, Patton, Devers, Hershey, Holcomb, and the Major King . . . and from top civilians Robert P. Patterson and War Manpower Commissioner Paul V. McNair - With a record of that kind in one war, the responsibility is obvious as we face what may become another war. The NRA must do its share in preparing the American civilian for the future . . . whether future turns out to be World War III, or merely a continuing collection of small wars scattered over the world. Already, cancellation of the NRA's convention and 1950 championships has echoed the beginning the 1942-45 program. And already in this, as in other wars, a Marine Corps General has restated an idea that is basic with us. Said Leatherneck General Edward Craig, after his troops had gone ashore at Pusan: 'It looks like a rifleman's war.' This 1950-style training of the NRA's will have to be different from the 1942-45 model . . . to deal with a whole new set of national and world conditions. The 1950 program must be applicable not only to the needs of national preparedness and the immediate demands of the armed forces, but to long-term problems as safety in the hunting fields and the basic concept of an armed, alert and peaceful America. The NRA's new program, as it unfolds in the coming months, must be something more then an answer to immediate needs. This time it must be a direct investment in a peaceful future. That we can't lose!

THE gentleman in California who has been so actively promoting the Alco Crime Promotion (his literature misquotes it as "Crime Prevention") Law is beginning to act and talk in the cheap, theatrical manner which, since time immemorial, has been the refuge of the poor sport when encountering unexpected opposition. "We have confessions from gun-runners in San Quentin and Folsom in which they declare that one of the easiest ways to circulate pistols in the underworld is to organize a gun club." * * * "The national rifle and pistol associations are responsible for the fact that there is not a real pistol law in the United States. What laws we have are useless, silly and in most cases deliberately drafted to further pistol sales to members of rifle and pistol associations and crooks." * * * "Permitting the heads of the National Rifle Association and the United States Revolver Association to draft our firearms legislation, as they admit they do, is as ridiculous as permitting the heads of the Chinese opium producers to draft our narcotic laws." * * * These are choice excerpts from recent statements given to California newspapers. Amazing innuendos, these, to be issuing from the lips of one upon whose honesty and fairness depends much of the effectiveness of California's penal system. The man who made those statements did not speak the truth. The descent to such statements can only be Evidence to the thinking people of California that a deliberate effort is being made to prevent logical discussion of the Alco proposals by throwing up between the sportsmen of the State and their neighbors and friends a screen of villification. The sportsmen who are opposing the Alco proposals have no intention of being drawn into any campaign of competitive mud-slinging. However, since Mr. Alco has seen fit to inject personalities into the fight, the dictates of good sportsmanship now require that all the cards be laid upon the table so far as personalities are concerned-after which we shall immediately return to the real business of pointing out that the Alco Bill, if enacted, will actually make gun-carrying by the criminal a safer matter than it is under the existing California Law, and will make it possible for the crook who has committed a crime while armed to be paroled from four to twenty-four years sooner than under the present law! And now to the unpleasant matter of clearing the record as to personalities. During the period from 1916 to 1919 there were a great many young men from California and elsewhere who were highly thought of at the time because they voluntarily donned uniforms and ventured whither they might be ordered in the belief that by doing so they were protecting their homes and womenfolk (as well as a certain percentage of slackers and chiselers) from foreign aggression. A considerable proportion of the "gun-club members" - now referred to as gun-runners or dupes for gun-runners - were so engaged. The present "heads of the National Rifle Association" (likened by Mr. Alco to Chinese opium smugglers) were taking part in the activities along with the others who thought it was the thing to do. And where was Mr. Alco at this important time? Why, he was petitioning the Supreme Court of the State of California to change his name from Olcovich to Alco, for reasons of "convenience!" There is the possibility that Mr. Alco may disclaim responsibility for some of the statements issued to the press. If so, then the responsibility falls upon the publicity chairman of the Alco Committee, whose present name is "Don Castle." During the five years beginning in 1928, when the California police first began ar-' resting him, he has been known also as D. C. Castlelake, D.C. Castle, and Din Castle. He claims to have been an Olympic Pistol Shot from South Africa, and to love pistols as only the expert can - but the South African Shooting Association has never heard of him. He claims to have studied the firearms problem for years past, and to be sincerely convinced of the need of outlawing the pistol in order to remove temptation from the path of the morally weak - but though he has a record of six arrests in four years in California, none of his operations were conducted while using a gun. Sent to San Quentin in June, 1932, with a sentence of from none to fourteen years, Castle was paroled in June, 1933, in spite of a five-year police record. Mr. Alco may deny responsibility for the published canards concerning honest sportsmen, but he cannot deny responsibility for permitting a criminal of this type to assume an extremely important position on the committee sponsoring the Alco Bill. How many of the well-meaning women, the judges, the prosecutors, who have been lending their names to the plausible "crime prevention bill," are going to bitterly resent being associated in the public mind with such personalities? One more reference for the record, and we shall drop the sorry subject for all time. The man, at least one of the men, who has given Alco much legal advice in the drafting of his proposed bill, and in subsequent moves, is a disbarred attorney who was convicted and subsequently paroled for a crime involving the misuse of funds. And a gun had nothing whatever to do with his succumbing to the criminal impulse. This man - who for reasons of "convenience" renounced the honorable name of his family; who admits that he got the idea for his proposed crime panacea from criminals; who permits canards (about honorable citizens to be released to the public press by a paroled convict- this man has the consummate nerve to seek the support of sincere, honorable women, who know little or nothing of his background prior to his political appointment to the State Prison Board, or of the criminals responsible for the conception, and now aiding the promotion, of his adroitly-titled "Crime Prevention Bill." Will Mr. Alco and his Publicity Chairman kindly return now to an explanation as to how their bill, reducing the penalties for committing crime while armed, and increasing the penalties only in the case of honest citizens, is such an outstanding improvement over the existing California Law? Will they explain why every crook in California should not prefer the Alco Bill to the existing Law? Will they explain why honorable citizens of California are accused of collusion with gun-runners when police records show no cases of such activity - whereas the public knows that criminals in two of Mr. Alco's State prisons have actually made guns within the prison walls? Is this gratuitous attack on sportsmen a smoke screen to make the public forget the San Quentin and Folsom-made guns, or to divert the minds of the public from the disgraceful record of pardons for vicious criminals which has been established while Mr. Alco has been in office?

Here at a time when the nation's gun owners should be gearing up for action, NRA's achievements over the past two years seem to have lulled them into a self-satisfied slumber and a false sense of security. Too many NRA members believe the war to defend America's firearm freedoms ended with the last congressional election. They think that because we defeated many anti-gun politicians and elected a pro-gun majority, we can call off the watchdogs and go home. NRA veterans will tell you that such thinking is an open invitation to disaster. They've been on the front lines when other apathy-prone troops deserted, and they know what it's like to face wave after wave of vicious attacks. Every time NRA members have felt comfortable enough to rest on their laurels, we've been bombarded with some of worst resurgences of anti-gun politicking, propaganda and legislation in our history. And it's all because we left our posts, dropped our guard and disregarded the ominous storm clouds gathering on the horizon. The enemies of the Second Amendment didn't go away. Instead they are regrouping. In fact their self-proclaimed leader, President Bill Clinton, has an ambitious anti-gun agenda he's determined to pass into law if he's elected to a second term. Right now most political pundits believe the President has at least a 50-50 chance of regaining the White House. If that happens, Clinton and his anti-gun cronies have been up-front about their plans to abolish your gun rights as quickly as possible. Nor have they been bashful about explaining how they plan to accomplish the task. Clinton's anti-gun agenda, which will be set into motion in a matter of months if we don't rise up, reads like this: The president has vowed to work for more anti-gun laws, to veto the repeal of gun bans he's already signed into law and to appoint judges who won't uphold the right to keep and bear arms. The president has already begun waging his own personal anti-gun crusade while on the campaign trail. This spring he's stumped for handgun registration, Canadian-style strict gun control and cabinet-level power to ban virtually all ammunition. Clinton has broadened his anti-gun vision to encompass international horizons. The president is pushing for a worldwide, United Nations-backed gun control campaign that would stress import bans on commonly owned handguns. In Congress, one of Clinton's chief anti-gun allies, Rep. Charles Schumer, is fighting for passage of a national one-gun-purchase-per-month gun rights rationing scheme. And in the U.S. Senate, Barbara Boxer is pushing for a ban on the domestic manufacture and possession of firearms that she's labeled as "junk guns" - whatever that arbitrary new buzzword means. Rep. Schumer and his media friends are working to ban all advertising by a number of leading firearms manufacturers. These are the same people who try to censor NRA advertising, especially when we seek to place ads that are favorable to the second Amendment and gun owners' rights. Sen. Dianne Feinstein, along with a cadre of fellow anti-gun senators, is working hard to block any effort to repeal Clinton gun bans already in place. It's one of the most ambitious an vicious anti-gun attacks in modern history, and it's only just begun. Meanwhile, some media know-it-alls claim our NRA membership appears soft, complacent, overconfident and unwilling to rise to this new threat. Make no mistake: NRA members need to come awake, spring to our feet and ready every means of defense at our disposal. Because whether you know it or not, this new and expanding anti-gun movement is bigger, tougher, smarter and better financed than any we've ever faced before. After their embarrassing defeat two years ago, they're out for revenge. So they've devoted all their resources to developing a coordinated strategy for attack, and to amassing the money, machinery' and manpower needed to carry their anti-gun agenda to victory. That's why it's absolutely crucial every one of you do your part to begin preparing our defenses now. That means join, renew or upgrade your NRA membership and get everyone else who cares about their rights to do the same. And please send the most generous contribution that you can make when you receive our call to action. Do not let the success we achieved in 1994 make you believe that our requests for extra contributions to defend your freedoms can be ignored this year. As the 1996 elections approach and the enemies of the Second Amendment set their forces in motion, it's time for every one of us to re-enlist for the fight. And dig in for the battles ahead.

Approximately one out of every five or six American males is a hunter. Few other sports offer as much to as many people. In terms of activity and wholesome adventure, hunting exercises the body and stimulates the mind. In financial terms, it with its ramifications of transportation, gear and arms is in the billion-dollar-industry class. The National Rifle Association is proud of its hunting members and proud that they stand for the best in this field of sport, just as its match competitors patriotically represent the United States in International and other competition and its collector-members keep alive the historical traditions of America. Like so much else in the United States today, hunting is beset by problems. If those problems are to be solved, and we believe they will be, the NRA ranks high among the organizations working to satisfactory solutions. For one thing, the NRA is doing its share to present the hunter in an appropriate and favorable light to the great non-hunting public. The first point in the NRA Hunter's Code of Ethics, to which more than four million graduates of the NRA Hunter Safety Training Program subscribe, provides that the hunter consider himself "an invited guest of the landowner" and behave so that he "may be welcome in the future." Those are among the most important words in hunting today. As cities expand, industries spread, and open land shrinks, the problem of finding a place to hunt becomes increasingly difficult. Every urban area is ringed by suburbs and much of the land around and beyond the suburbs is posted with "No Hunting" and "No Trespassing" signs. For the latter, hunters in general have only themselves to blame. Most of the blame, it should be said, attaches to the unduly carefree sportsmen who are neither NRA Members nor NRA-indoctrinated. These are the types who blast at signs, break fences, disregard regulations, and roam at random without permission of land-owners. In numbers, they are, fortunately, relatively few. In the damage that they do, they might just as well be the hordes of Genghis Khan or Attila the Hun. The third point of the NRA Hunter's Code of Ethics provides that the hunter will not only obey all game laws and regulations himself but will insist that his companions "do likewise." While NRA Members, who constitute a relatively small proportion of the 15 to 20 million hunters in the U.S., can hardly police the entire field, they can make their influence felt for the better in this respect. The surest way to prevent the closing off of privately-owned areas where game abounds is to demonstrate to the owners of the areas that their property, safety and personal wishes will be respected. A universal attitude to that effect could make "No Hunting" and "No Trespassing" signs vanish almost overnight, instead of breaking out over the countryside like an epidemic rash. Much of the solution to the problem is so simple. It lies in things as elementary as remembering that the firearm in your hands is a responsibility, not a toy; in acting like a grownup; in remembering that alcohol and guns do not mix. It can all be summed up in one word: Behave. Like a hunter. Like a man. Like a good American.

"It's a free country," or "There ought be a law." Which of those hoary old credos do you lean toward? I bring the subject up because of a barrage of new government restrictions, either proposed or passed, that have been featured in the media in the past month or so. Four that brought about this column are: - the banning of three wheeled all-terrain vehicles, under the impetus of the Justice Department and the Consumer Product Safety Commission, - a study group's recommendation that the Securities and Exchange Commission "should take over regulation of stock index futures - and that rules should be tougher" following the October 19 crash, - a proposal before the Massachusetts Legislature to label alcoholic beverages (beer, liquor, wine) as dangerous to the consumer's health - and, a ban on smoking on commercial flights in California as well as nationally on flights under two hours duration. While most of us recognize the need for a degree of regulation in civilized societies - you'd have a hard time convincing many of us that airline deregulation has improved flying or that the break up of AT&T has helped phone service - we fear the loss of individual freedoms purely for the sake of satisfying someone's idea of what constitutes "the public good." Without using this entire page to list just a fraction of the more common infringements on our freedoms perpetuated by the social planners, we can add to the aforementioned examples of mandated "protections" seat belt laws, motorcycle helmets, smoke detectors, zoning regulations, etc. Before you pick up the telephone, typewriter or pen to explain the important benefits to be derived from many of the above, please understand that I question not the advantages linked to such restraints but only the fact they are imposed from without rather than being prompted by our own common sense and good judgment. Obviously the thing that struck my hot button in the dramatic increase of government encroachment upon Americans life-style during what we hoped would be a conservative period, is the matter of our Second Amendment rights. While NRA has historically recognized and respected the inherent authority of government to curtail criminal conduct through the laws governing our nation, we have insisted that the controls be on those who would abuse the rights of others and not upon the rights themselves. While I doubt any of us believe smoking is good for one's health, I would remind you that before smoking was banned in certain public areas the cigarette packs were first labeled as being hazardous to one's health. Is the next step a total ban on consumer purchase of tobacco? And if so, tell me what great public service will be accomplished by making it a crime to puff on one's pipe beside a lovely camp fire high in the Rockies? Party to our daily efforts to defend gun owners' rights against the incursions of the antis is the clear and present danger that those lawmakers who listen to the pleas for "reasonable regulations" intentionally or unintentionally diminish our freedoms. The siren song of an ordered society is oftimes attractive to those who don't have the commitment and resolve to deal with the problems natural to a free society, and they misrepresent the comment made by former U.S. Senator Margaret Chase Smith (Maine) that "Given the choice between anarchy and dictatorship the American public will choose dictatorship." That distinguished lady was comparing dictatorship to anarchy, not to freedom. I suppose the fact that elected officials are by definition lawmakers encourages the belief that the more laws passed the better the lawmaker. Everyone of us can bear witness to too many cases where the exact opposite has been true.
